1l88jfc.text: The pCloud Pass password manager suffered a cyberattack, with users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts even with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled. The incident was first reported by numerous pCloud customers who began receiving email notifications informing them that a new device had connected to their pCloud Pass accounts. In two Reddit threads, customers worldwide reported receiving notifications warning that an unfamiliar device named "pd" connected to their account from the IP address 45.131.244.7 in Luxembourg, which users say belongs to pCloud's own infrastructure. pCloud Pass warning of a new device connecting to an account Source: BleepingComputer Several customers reported receiving the alerts despite having two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled on their accounts. However, when customers checked their accounts for connected devices, some found no unfamiliar devices listed. Other pCloud customers reported receiving the same notifications despite never having used the company's password manager, including one who said the notification was sent to an email address associated with a pCloud storage account they had requested be deleted almost a year ago. In response to the reports, pCloud confirmed its password manager had suffered a cyberattack, which the company says was quickly contained. "A cyberattack targeting pCloud Pass occurred, which was promptly contained by the pCloud team," reads pCloud's statement. "Unfortunately, a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and login attempts were made. Our system sends a notification automatically to each of these addresses." pCloud says the attack was isolated to its password manager and that its cloud storage services were not affected. The company says that passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass have not been compromised, explaining that the data is encrypted on customers' devices and can only be decrypted using their master passwords. However, pCloud did not disclose whether any encrypted password vaults were accessed or stolen during the attack. This matters because threat actors who obtain encrypted password vaults could try to crack them offline without being subject to the service's login rate limits or two-factor authentication protections. This was demonstrated in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults. Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak or reused master passwords to access stored cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases. A reader who contacted BleepingComputer also noted that the "Open settings" link in the email notifications pointed to passqa1.pcloud.com, which appears to be a quality assurance (QA) environment rather than the password manager's production website. BleepingComputer confirmed that the link pointed to the same hostname in a copy of the notification shared with us. In its statement, pCloud also discussed how advancements in artificial intelligence are accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, but did not specifically state that this was an AI-powered attack. The company is also warning customers to watch for phishing attacks, stating that it will never ask for their master passwords or recovery words over email, phone, or chat. The pCloud Pass incident is the latest in a series of cyberattacks impacting password managers this month. Earlier in November, mSeven Software warned mSecure customers to change stored passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys after a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database. On Wednesday, 1Password disclosed a data breach after a threat actor compromised an employee's GitHub account and deployed malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data. However, 1Password said customers' password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 18aoqub.text: Medical technology company Boston Scientific is sending data breach notices to individuals affected by a cyberattack on the firm. According to a notification sample Boston Scientific shared with U.S. authorities, the hacker used social engineering in a voice phishing (vishing) attack to gain access to the company's cloud infrastructure. The attack exposed cloud-based applications and cloud-hosted data between May 7 and 1. The company became aware of the unauthorized access on May 12, and the investigation determined that a data breach occurred on November 5. Individuals in multiple U.S. states have been impacted, exposing personal details and medical information. According to the Texas Attorney General breach portal, the incident exposed information from 117,789 people, which included: Full name Physical address Social Security Number (SSN) Government-issued ID number (e.g., passport, state ID card) Medical information Health insurance information Date of birth The letter sent to impacted individuals specifies that patient medical records and data from remote monitoring systems, connected medical devices, and clinical case management or workflow applications were not exposed. Boston Scientific is a Massachusetts-based medical device maker whose products include stents, catheters, pacemakers, defibrillators, and endoscopes. It is one of the world’s largest medical device manufacturers, with more than 59,000 employees, 13 manufacturing facilities, and a presence in 127 countries. In 2025, Boston Scientific reported more than $20 billion in revenue. The company said there was no disruption to manufacturing, ordering, distribution, or service to patients and healthcare providers as a result of this incident. It also said the incident had no impact on operations, performance, remote monitoring, or the safety of its products and medical devices. Boston Scientific says it contained the incident, investigated with outside cybersecurity experts, and notified law enforcement. The notification does not offer free credit monitoring to impacted individuals but recommends using free credit reports and considering placing fraud alerts and credit freezes. Second breach in 2026 The breach is the second cybersecurity incident this year. On August 25, Boston Scientific disclosed a cyberattack that caused network outages and a global operational disruption for the company, including to order processing and shipping. CrowdStrike’s investigation determined that the attacker breached an internet-facing network device and pivoted to a limited part of the on-premises IT environment. However, the investigators found no evidence that the attackers compromised cloud applications. BleepingComputer contacted Boston Scientific to learn more about the most recent incident, and a spokesperson confirmed that it is unrelated to the August 2026 intrusion. The spokesperson declined to share additional details. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. juatfw.text: A zero-day vulnerability in the Cacti network monitoring platform has been publicly disclosed, along with a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers. The exploit, dubbed "4HTTP2SHELL" (previously 4HTTP2ROOT), was published on Thanksgiving Day by a cybersecurity researcher known as ek0ms savi0r from the Church of Malware, who demonstrated how the vulnerability can be exploited using just four HTTP requests. Cacti is an open-source network monitoring and graphing tool used to monitor the performance of servers, routers, switches, firewalls, and other network infrastructure. Because the software can store credentials and SNMP passphrases used to access or read data from monitored devices, compromising a Cacti server could potentially give attackers access to other systems on a corporate network. The researcher published a technical write-up, a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, and a video demonstrating the attack in a GitHub repository named "Sad Girls 0day Club." "I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests. No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface," explains the researcher. The vulnerability stems from weak input validation that allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject SQL statements into the application's database and modify commands executed by Cacti's real-time poller. The attack requires the Cacti guest account to be enabled but does not require attackers to possess valid credentials. While the researcher demonstrated the exploit providing root access to a vulnerable server, cybersecurity firm watchTowr explains that the privileges gained through exploitation depend on the account running the Cacti web server and poller processes. In many deployments, this could be a low-privileged web server account rather than root. Cybersecurity firm RavenAI explains that the attack abuses weak validation of guest users' graph display settings, resulting in a stored SQL injection vulnerability. The attack involves an attacker saving malicious SQL statements in a guest user's graph display preferences, which are stored in Cacti's database. When Cacti processes these saved preferences, it executes the SQL statements, allowing the attacker to modify the poller's configuration and cause it to run malicious operating system commands. The researcher tested the exploit against Cacti Core 1.2.31, but it is unclear whether earlier versions are also vulnerable. In a separate post on the GitHub repository, ek0ms savi0r expressed frustration with how companies handle vulnerability disclosures, describing years of security reports being dismissed or closed as duplicates, expected behavior, or issues that could not be reproduced. "Security researchers are not the bad guys. We're the ones trying to help. We're the ones who read the docs, wrote the repro, and sent the packet capture," wrote the researcher. "We get cracked because we get gaslit for years by billion dollar companies that treat disclosure like a PR problem." In an Instagram post announcing the Cacti exploit, the researcher shared a video demonstration of the PoC and said that the vulnerability was not reported to Cacti before being released. Until a patch is released, administrators are advised to deactivate the Cacti guest account and restrict access to the application's web interface to trusted networks. Administrators should also review poller configurations for unexpected commands and examine application logs for warnings involving non-numeric values in graph display settings, which could indicate attempted exploitation. As of November 27, there have been no reports of the vulnerability being exploited in attacks. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. wxp5i4.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 27, 2026Cyber Espionage / Government Security A Vietnam-sponsored hacking group has been attributed to attacks targeting Southeast Asian military, government, and legislative organizations with an aim to gather intelligence on South China Sea defense and military agreements. The previously undocumented incursion set, detailed by SOCRadar, has been codenamed WeaveLotus. The activity is assessed to have comprised five intrusions in Thailand and the Philippines and reconnaissance efforts against Indonesian government organizations. "Initial access was achieved primarily by exploiting web application vulnerabilities and default credentials in open-source software, including GeoServer, JasperReports, osTicket, and exposed Laravel debug mode configurations," SOCRadar said in an analysis published Thursday. "The threat actor established persistent internal network access using reverse SSH tunnels and moved laterally into downstream networks and applications." The links to Vietnam are based on the presence of native Vietnamese-language code comments, operational activity aligning with UTC+07:00 working hours, regional strategic targeting, and custom scripting. The sustained campaign, codenamed RedOps, was observed between August and September 2026. The threat actor has also been observed conducting open-source intelligence (OSINT), setting up automated Bing search scripts that scraped news and documents on military agreements involving the Philippines, China, and the U.S., with a particular emphasis on the South China Sea, a region of strategic and geopolitical importance. Earlier this August, Hunt.io disclosed details of another cyber espionage operation undertaken by a suspected Chinese threat actor targeting a nuclear research organization and a marine engineering and shipbuilding company to steal sensitive documents after gaining access through known security vulnerabilities. "Following the OSINT phase, the operators enumerated government, military, and legislative entities across the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia, compromising targets in Thailand and the Philippines across five confirmed intrusions," SOCRadar said. "Activity against Indonesian targets did not progress beyond reconnaissance." "The core objective of RedOps appears to be the exfiltration of internal records and documents from Southeast Asian governments in support of Vietnam's foreign policy and military intelligence priorities." A brief overview of the intrusion activity is as follows - Thai military organization, which likely involved the exploitation of a critical GeoServer flaw (CVE-2024-36401, CVSS score: 9.8) to deploy a SOCKS5 proxy and open a reverse SSH tunnel, followed by hands-on reconnaissance, persistence, and unauthenticated access to Directus CMS API's file collection and asset download endpoints to enumerate records and download a subset of those records. The threat actor also ran Optical Character Recognition (OCR) on the collected data to extract English and Thai text from PNG images, and unsuccessfully attempted to gain access to surveillance video feeds hosted on Wowza to possibly gain real-time visibility into military operations. Thai legislative organization, which involved the attacker leveraging an exposed JasperReports server with default administrative credentials (jasperadmin:jasperadmin) to upload a malicious report that ultimately executed SQL scripts on the backend Microsoft SQL Server and then deleted the report to cover up the tracks. The SQL commands, in turn, employed xp_cmdshell to launch a reverse SSH SOCKS proxy tunnel over port 443 to WeaveLotus infrastructure ("172.235.245[.]49"). The attackers deployed a lightweight Python C2 server to automate post-exploitation and targeted a third-party document management system (DMS) by launching password spraying attacks using real employee names paired with National ID numbers as passwords. Once authenticated, the attackers collected the entire system configuration, the complete application user directory comprising 1,502 records), along with system audit logs and 5,000 ZIP archives containing sensitive data. Thai government organization, which involved the attacker gaining root SSH access to a server running Keycloak 3.4 and dumping its credential database, following cracking the PBKDF2-SHA256 hashes offline with wordlists built around Thai Buddhist Era years and then validating them in real-time against the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) token endpoint. The working accounts belonged to users from various Thai ministries and agencies, with two of them granting the attackers administrative privileges. The valid credentials were then used to pull 349,782 records from a downstream application that contained national strategy alignment, reform directives, masterplan targets, sustainable development goals, and five-year fiscal plans, among others. Philippine government organization A, which involved the exploitation of an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in osTicket (CVE-2021-42235, CVSS score: 9.8) to extract database schemas and dump usernames, email addresses, and bcrypt password hashes for registered staff accounts. Philippine government organization B, which probed a web application built on the Laravel framework to obtain server paths and fragments of application source code, ultimately revealing directories tied to an internal project-management and budgeting system. "WeaveLotus conducted broad reconnaissance against Indonesian government agencies [between August and September 2026]," SOCRadar said. "The operators began with passive reconnaissance, harvesting Certificate Transparency (CT) logs via CertSpotter and crt.sh, before progressing to active Nmap port scans, VPN service fingerprinting (targeting Palo Alto GlobalProtect, Ivanti Connect Secure / Pulse Secure, Cisco ASA, and Fortinet FortiGate), and IMAP/POP3 banner grabbing across more than 30 organizations." The RedOps campaign is notable for the fact that it has only singled out government, military, and legislative institutions in the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia, with no evidence that private-sector entities were targeted. This indicates that the activity is consistent with state-directed intelligence collection. "The RedOps campaign illustrates how a suspected Vietnam-linked espionage operation leveraged exposed applications, weak authentication controls, and persistent network tunnels to conduct intelligence collection across Southeast Asian government and military environments," SOCRadar said. "The recovered tooling and operational artifacts provide valuable insight into the actor's methods, while the available evidence supports tracking WeaveLotus as a distinct activity cluster without conclusively establishing state sponsorship."

11k0tm5.text: Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department. According to Reuters, the intrusion was discovered within the past month during an upgrade of the cloud platform, disrupting application migrations and software updates. Launched in 2017, Cloud One is an enterprise cloud computing platform managed by the US Air Force that allows Department of Defense agencies to host and manage applications supporting military operations, personnel management, logistics, and maintenance. According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information. US Cyber Command has reportedly been called in to assess the impact, with the attackers, scope of the attack, and whether any data was stolen currently unknown. The Air Force declined to comment on the security or operational status of the affected systems, telling Reuters that it continuously takes measures to protect its information, systems, and mission capabilities. The reported Air Force breach follows other cybersecurity incidents disclosed over the past week targeting US federal agencies. On November 21, it was revealed that hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. The database contains information on wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and other criminal justice records. The intrusion came two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group breached FBI systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in the agency's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov. Earlier this week, hackers also reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The incident also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). Hours after the CIA breach was reported, the US Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to its systems. It is unclear whether any of the recently disclosed federal government breaches are connected. AI-powered hacking tools fuel cyberattacks The CIA breach was reportedly conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing platform, which the FBI recently warned was being used to automate cyberattacks worldwide. In an advisory, the FBI said multiple threat actors had used ARTEX since at least August 2026 in attacks targeting government, defense, healthcare, financial, and technology organizations. ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that uses AI agents to automate various stages of a cyberattack, including discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, escalating privileges, and stealing data. The framework integrates with external AI models from Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, Grok, and others, allowing attackers to conduct autonomous attacks against organizations with minimal human intervention. According to the FBI, some ARTEX-powered intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. The platform was used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940 in an October attack targeting ConnectWise's Cloud Backup service. Cybersecurity firm Huntress identified at least 162 compromised Microsoft 365 customer tenants during the campaign. Other attacks linked to ARTEX include: Attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information of approximately 67,000 people. A South Korean hacking campaign targeting more than 90 organizations, resulting in the theft of approximately 8.2 million data records and the arrest of seven suspects. A cyberespionage campaign attributed by CrowdStrike to a Chinese hacking group tracked as Vapor Panda, which targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries and compromised at least nine. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX management consoles, with the number believed to be much higher. It remains unknown whether ARTEX or other AI-powered hacking tools were used in the attacks against the Air Force, FBI, or FinCEN. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. m2t4s5.text: When discussing IT infrastructure security, the focus is usually on firewalls, EDR, backup, vulnerability management, and network segmentation. However, all of them are effective only under one condition — if the infrastructure itself is under control. Incidents often begin not with the exploitation of a vulnerability or bypassing protection systems, but with shortcomings in basic infrastructure management. Every virtual machine, server, access, and IP address must have an owner, a lifetime, and a controlled path for creation and deletion. When management processes are opaque, the infrastructure itself becomes a source of information security risks, and security tools have to operate over an unknown environment and merely contain the consequences. This principle is equally critical for enterprise companies and service providers — regardless of whether the platform serves internal services, development teams, or external customers, a loss of control over administration can lead to the compromise of the entire environment. Why Security Grows Out of Manageability In modern IT infrastructure, hundreds of systems run on the same resources, and the environment itself is constantly changing — dozens of services are created, scaled, and deleted daily. In such conditions, provisioning comes to the fore. Deploying a new virtual machine without a regulation and recording the owner leaves "forgotten" VMs in the environment. They do not receive updates, fall out of monitoring, and become an easy entry point for an attacker. Centralized access management is no less critical. The platform must delineate the rights of users and administrators and record all operations; otherwise, excessive rights accumulate, allowing attackers to move laterally across the network. We should not forget about the isolation of environments — the resources of different customers at a hosting provider, or internal systems, external services, and development environments in corporate IT infrastructure. If isolation is violated, an incident in the test environment can affect business-critical services. All this is impossible without lifecycle control — linking capacity allocation to billing, quotas, and timely deletion of resources, so that outdated accounts and "abandoned" IP addresses do not remain in the network. Finally, manageability is impossible without accurate accounting of the physical layer: the appearance, decommissioning, and movement of servers between racks and sites. Inaccurate accounting generates unaccounted servers and loss of control over security configurations. Therefore, the foundation of information security is the transparency of resource management throughout their entire lifecycle. Migration from VMware and the Change in the Management Model Broadcom's change in licensing policy forced companies to reconsider their infrastructure strategies and look for alternatives to VMware — for example, considering Proxmox VE, OpenStack, and other open-source solutions. However, migrating to a new platform requires more than just the correct transfer of virtual machines. Over the years of working with VMware, many have become accustomed to perceiving it as a single whole — virtualization, resource management, access, automation, and accounting. When migrating to another stack, it quickly becomes clear that virtualization is not equal to infrastructure management: the hypervisor is just one element, and the remaining functions have to be assembled from several independent solutions. Proxmox and OpenStack solve virtualization tasks on their own, but without additional software, they do not cover operational processes and control over the other layers of the environment. As a result, organizations have to independently integrate equipment management systems, resource accounting, access control, and inventory. The more individual components in the infrastructure, the harder it is to maintain unified security policies — risks arise of losing a unified RBAC, end-to-end inventory, action auditing, and automation. Therefore, it is important to view migration from VMware not just as a change of hypervisor, but as a revision of the entire infrastructure management model: if centralized control, automation, and lifecycle management are postponed for later, over time they become a source of new risks. Which Processes a Management Platform Must Cover After abandoning VMware, companies face the main question — how to rebuild infrastructure management. When choosing a replacement, it is important to look not only at the capabilities of the hypervisor itself but also at what operational and security processes the chosen solution can cover and what additional integrations will be required. At the foundation, there should be centralized management of the entire environment from a single interface and role-based access control (RBAC). Equally important are the isolation of environments or customers, transparent resource accounting, and control of the entire lifecycle — from the creation of a virtual machine to its deletion and the revocation of access. Also, the platform must manage the physical layer of servers and automate routine operations. Such an architecture can be built in different ways: assembled from separate open-source tools and independently solving the issue of their integration, or by choosing a ready-made comprehensive solution. Regardless of the approach, it is precisely the coverage of these processes that returns the infrastructure to the transparency and manageability that the VMware ecosystem previously provided. How to Build a Unified Management Environment To avoid assembling infrastructure management from disparate systems, all these processes can be combined within a single ISPsystem product stack. In this architecture, VMmanager is responsible for virtualization, DCImanager for the physical level of the infrastructure, and BILLmanager acts as the end-to-end layer for resource provisioning, quotas, accounting, and FinOps. VMmanager automates the lifecycle of virtual machines, including deployment with a preinstalled software stack, and scales up to 60,000 VMs and 700 nodes in a single environment. Network isolation based on VxLAN supports more than 16 million isolated segments between geographically distributed sites, and a self-service portal is provided for users. In parallel, DCImanager provides centralized management and full inventory of the physical layer in multi-vendor environments — from servers to switches and UPSs. The platform checks equipment health and disk S.M.A.R.T. data, configures BMC, performs secure drive wiping, automatically installs the OS, monitors hardware status, and controls warranty periods. All three products integrate seamlessly with each other and work as a single environment, and if necessary, can interact with external solutions — for example, with OpenStack. BILLmanager acts as the end-to-end layer here: it links the provisioning of IT resources with authorization and accounting, allows assembling combined services, and implements showback and chargeback mechanisms. The built-in BI module with customizable dashboards for analyzing resource utilization deserves special attention. In a corporate environment, it helps to find "abandoned" capacity in time, which development teams forget to delete after completing tasks — such servers do not sit idle without updates and control, and the company reduces hardware and license costs. How Implementing a Unified Management Environment Affects IT Infrastructure Security When the processes of managing virtualization, physical equipment, and the resource lifecycle are linked into a single environment, security ceases to be just a set of protective tools and becomes the result of systemic manageability. Information security and operations teams get a transparent picture of the entire environment — from the physical server to the virtual machine, its owner, and the history of changes, which directly reduces the number of "blind spots." Automation of provisioning, delineation of rights, and control over resource lifetimes reduce the risk of errors in issuing access, the appearance of unaccounted servers, and the retention of "forgotten" virtual machines. This also simplifies the migration from VMware itself: companies do not just replace the hypervisor, but build a transparent and manageable operating model. As a result, infrastructure security relies not only on individual security tools but also on the management system itself, which makes the environment predictable, controllable, and resilient to risks. gsx3k6.text: Japan’s education ministry disclosed earlier this week that hackers had breached its government procurement system, potentially exposing records containing business information and email addresses. The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) said it detected the intrusion on October 1, nearly two months before publicly disclosing the incident. An investigation found that hackers may have obtained information stored in the system’s database. The potentially compromised data includes nearly 1,700 email addresses and 164,000 records containing company names, the names of employees and other business information, the ministry said in a statement Wednesday. The affected system is used to publish information about government tenders, contracts and procurement opportunities. The potentially exposed business information relates to companies eligible to participate in the ministry’s bidding processes. The ministry said it had blocked all communications between the affected system and internal and external networks and found no evidence that the potentially compromised information has been publicly disclosed or misused. The incident was reported to Japan’s data protection authorities, and the ministry is continuing its investigation in coordination with relevant government agencies. It has not publicly identified the perpetrators or disclosed how they gained access to its systems. “We will continue to investigate the incident in close cooperation with the relevant authorities and take appropriate action,” MEXT said. This is the latest cybersecurity incident affecting major Japanese companies and public institutions in recent months. Earlier this week, Japanese railway operator Keio Corporation said a ransomware attack in September may have compromised the personal information of more than 11 million customers, business partners, employees and job applicants. The ransomware group Qilin, believed to have Russian origins, claimed responsibility for the attack. McDonald’s Japan also recently disclosed a breach involving a database linked to its official mobile app. The compromised information included customers’ purchase histories, IP addresses, internal customer identification numbers and mobile device location data. Earlier this month, the city of Osaka disclosed that a breach involving a third-party technology provider had exposed more than 1 million email addresses associated with an online platform for municipal services. Other major Japanese companies that have reported cybersecurity incidents in recent months include telecommunications giant KDDI, the Japanese unit of U.S. insurer Aflac, electronics manufacturer Nidec and brewer Sapporo Holdings. There is no indication that these incidents are connected. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. 7to4jf.text: German software giant SAP confirmed a cybersecurity incident following reports that hackers infiltrated its software development infrastructure, potentially gaining access to the company’s source code. In a statement to Recorded Future News on Friday, SAP said it had identified suspicious activity and immediately taken steps to protect its customers and secure its services. The company did not disclose the nature or extent of the intrusion. “Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data,” SAP said. “We will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.” German magazine Der Spiegel first reported the incident Thursday, citing internal company communications and sources familiar with the matter. According to the magazine, hackers targeted SAP’s software development environment hosted on GitHub, obtaining employee authentication tokens that allowed them to copy and modify the company’s source code. The German Press Agency (dpa), which independently reviewed portions of internal SAP communication, reported that the company had alerted employees to suspicious activity within its GitHub environment several days before the incident became public. Employees were advised to assess whether they needed to change their login credentials or take additional security precautions. SAP launched an internal incident response operation code-named “Project Granite,” according to German business newspaper Handelsblatt. The company’s emergency security measures reportedly affected several software development teams. SAP restricted access to GitHub, halted automated development processes and replaced digital keys used to verify that its software was genuine and had not been tampered with. It remains unclear whether the hackers accessed SAP’s proprietary source code or whether any altered code ended up in software delivered to customers. SAP has not publicly identified who was behind the attack, how the hackers gained access to its systems or whether the incident has been fully contained. SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software companies whose products are used by businesses and public institutions worldwide to manage critical operations, including accounting, procurement, supply chains and human resources. The incident follows a separate software supply chain attack in April, when hackers injected malicious code into several open-source software packages developed by SAP in an attempt to steal sensitive information from developers and automated software development environments. It is unclear whether the two incidents are connected. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

54xb9e.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 27, 2026Malware / Social Engineering Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber attack in which a threat actor leveraged a Microsoft Store application to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) called Vinci RAT. The intrusion, according to eSentire, begins with a redirection to a bogus site for a sniping tool ("snipp.codes-team[.]com"), from where a Microsoft-signed installer called "Snipping-Tool.exe" is downloaded. Executing the binary leads to the installation of Setup Assistant, an Electron-based application published on the Microsoft Store by ETPS Ltd. "The application was heavily obfuscated, maintained communication with C2 [command-and-control] infrastructure, monitored the victim's Downloads folder, and supported execution of C2-supplied PowerShell and JavaScript," eSentire said. "This access was used to launch a malicious PowerShell stager, establish persistence through a scheduled task, and retrieve a previously undocumented PowerShell-based RAT." Once installed, Setup Assistant acts as a backdoor and is designed to run obfuscated JavaScript that allows it to contact the C2 server at "setup-assistant[.]com" and retrieve arbitrary PowerShell or JavaScript code, ultimately resulting in the deployment of the RAT by means of a stager. Vinci RAT, as the malware is called, is equipped to fingerprint the host, enumerate installed security tools, facilitate remote and reverse shell access, deliver files, and execute shellcode, DLL, EXE, and PowerShell payloads. Interestingly, the arbitrary PowerShell or JavaScript execution is triggered by means of two methods - Monitor for file names in the victim's Downloads directory by matching them against a predefined list specified in a C2-retrieved configuration ("MSTeamsSetup.exe" and "Reader_install.exe"). If a match is found, it sends an HTTP POST request to the C2 server and executes the response. The C2 server initiates an update action via the URL setup-assistant[.]com/api/update-status?device=<victim_id>" The Vinci RAT stager is responsible for running a PowerShell command that disables the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI), generates a unique victim identifier, establishes communication with a C2 server ("monkeysholder[.]info/api.php"), set up persistence via a scheduled task that runs every 10 minutes, and downloads the RAT payload. Further analysis of the root domain "codes-team[.]com" has identified additional sub-domains that suggest that the threat actors are spoofing software download pages for legitimate applications like Microsoft Teams and Roblox - roblx.codes-team[.]com teams.codes-team[.]com teamsmac.codes-team[.]com teams-bing.codes-team.com As of writing, Setup Assistant is no longer accessible on Microsoft Software. It was first released on June 1, 2026, while the "codes-team[.]com" domain was registered in late March 2026. It remains unclear whether the threat actors themselves took down the app in response to the public disclosure or whether Microsoft removed it, as eSentire noted that the tech giant had failed to take action despite reporting the app through its abuse form on November 10, 2026, responding that it was "not a violation of our terms." "The campaign highlights how attackers are combining search-engine redirection, fake software download pages, obfuscated Electron applications, and trusted software distribution channels to gain persistent access to victim environments," the Canadian cybersecurity company said.

x3vjg3.text: Microsoft will remove the WSUS server role from Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system. Introduced in 2005 as Software Update Services (SUS), WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) lets IT administrators manage and distribute updates for Microsoft products across corporate networks with many Windows devices. It gives admins centralized control over the updates, rather than having each device download them individually from Microsoft's servers. Microsoft has officially deprecated WSUS in September 2024, but said that it still plans to maintain functionality and continue publishing updates through the channel. The change affects enterprise environments that rely on WSUS to manage updates delivered to many devices but does not impact home users or those using Microsoft Configuration Manager. In a recently updated support document, Microsoft went even further and confirmed that Windows Server 2028 removes the WSUS server role altogether. "WSUS remains available and supported in earlier Windows Server releases, including Windows Server 2025, for the duration of each release's support lifecycle. You can continue to use WSUS on those releases to manage updates for supported Windows client and Windows Server releases, which includes updates to Windows Server 2028," it said. "Microsoft recognizes the need to manage updates in disconnected and highly controlled environments. We're invested in supporting these scenarios and we'll share more as the work progresses." Businesses are now encouraged to adopt cloud-based solutions, such as Windows Autopatch, Microsoft Intune, and Azure Update Manager, for keeping endpoints and servers on their network up to date. "While the WSUS role remains available in Windows Server 2025, we recommend organizations transition to cloud tools, including including Windows Autopatch and Microsoft Intune for client update management and Azure Update Manager for server update management," Microsoft's Nir Froimovici said in September 2024. "Remember: WSUS remains operational but is no longer investing in new features." Windows Server 2028 also removes VBScript (disabled by default in Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10) and the legacy Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC) utility (deprecated in Windows Server 2012 and Windows 10 21H1) to thwart a wide range of malware and attack tactics abusing them. Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) support, deprecated with the release of Windows Server 2022 in August 2021, is also being removed in the next Windows Server version, as Microsoft announced a year ago. Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028 last week at the Ignite 2026 conference, and it can be tested by registering for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or applying to enroll in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access. duuzfj.text: Most security metrics are not built to be used. They are built to be shown. Somewhere between the quarterly review and the next status update, a set of numbers gets assembled that looks reassuring in a room and tells almost no one what is actually happening across the environment that week. Someone pulls them together the week before, cleans them up, and presents a picture of a program that is, as of that one morning, fine. This is not a failure of effort. Security teams are doing the work, often times more of it than anyone outside the team realizes. The problem is that the reporting cycle rewards the snapshot, and a snapshot is a memory, not a measurement. It tells you how things looked on the day you looked. It says very little about the weeks in between, and risk does not keep to a reporting schedule. Gathering the Picture Is the Hard Part, and It Is Getting Harder The conversation about security metrics usually jumps straight to which numbers matter. That skips the part that actually hurts. Before anyone can report a single metric, someone has to go and gather it, and today that is a genuinely painful job. The information needed to describe a security posture is scattered across dozens of systems that were never meant to talk to each other. Cloud accounts, identity providers, endpoints, code repositories, ticketing tools, each one holds a piece. Pulling those pieces together usually means logging into one console after another, exporting spreadsheets, taking screenshots, and stitching it all by hand into something presentable. It takes days. It eats the time of people who were hired to do security, not data entry. And by the time the picture is assembled, parts of it are already out of date, because the environment kept changing while the deck was being built. So the metric that lands in the review is not really a measurement of where things stand. It is a measurement of where things stood, filtered through however long it took to collect. (And filtered, quietly, toward whatever looked defensible that week.) Attackers Are Not Working on a Quarterly Cadence. With AI, They Are Faster Than Ever. Here is why the stale snapshot has gone from a weakness to a real liability. The people trying to get in have changed speed. AI has handed attackers a serious acceleration. Reconnaissance that used to take a skilled operator days now runs in minutes. Phishing that used to read as obviously fake now arrives fluent and personalized at scale. Known weaknesses get found and probed almost as fast as they appear. The attack side has automated the slow parts, and the result is adversaries who move in hours, iterate constantly, and do not pause politely between your reporting cycles. Now put the two timelines next to each other. On one side, a picture of your security that is gathered by hand, a few times a year, and is slightly stale the moment it is finished. On the other, an adversary moving at machine speed, every day, including the long quiet stretch between your last review and your next one. That gap was always uncomfortable. Against AI-accelerated attackers, it is the whole game. The Real Shift Is From Reporting to Visibility The fix is not a better slide. It is being able to see where you actually stand, continuously, without a person having to go assemble it first. That is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to confuse with detection. This is not about catching the attacker in the act. It is about never losing sight of your own environment in the first place, knowing what you have, what is covered, what changed, and where the gaps are, as a living picture rather than a quarterly photograph. Continuous visibility into the real environment, pulled straight from the systems that already hold the data, is what turns a security posture from something you reconstruct under deadline into something you can simply look at, any day, and trust. This is the problem Anecdotes was built to solve. Instead of a person logging into one console after another and rebuilding the picture by hand, it connects directly to the systems a company already runs, the cloud accounts, identity providers, code repositories, and the hundreds of other tools where the real state actually lives, and pulls the information straight from the source. The picture assembles itself and stays current, so the question stops being how many days it will take to gather and becomes simply what the data says right now. And to be clear about what that is and is not, it does not chase the attacker for you. It makes sure you are never the last to know what your own environment looks like. When the picture is always current, the work changes shape. Nobody spends the week before the review gathering. The number is just there, today's number, and the team spends its time acting on what it says instead of proving it exists. Start With One None of this requires rebuilding everything at once, and anyone who says it does is selling something. Pick one thing worth seeing clearly, coverage, say, or how long exposures stay open. Connect it to the source so it keeps itself current. Watch it for a month, and let it tell you something uncomfortable. Security is not a thing that is true on review day. It is true, or it is not, on an ordinary Tuesday, when no one is looking and last quarter's slide is gathering dust in a shared drive. And on that Tuesday, the attackers are not waiting. The teams that stay ahead are not the ones with the best-looking dashboards. They are the ones who can see where they stand at any moment, without having to go dig for it first.

bemrmj.text: The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites. Last week, Drupal patched a remote code execution (RCE) flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165 / Fail2Install) that lets anonymous users take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer. While the security issue wasn't initially flagged as being abused in the wild, an update to the original security advisory warned that threat actors began exploiting it one day after patches were released. The new security issue (CVE-2026-136716), patched one week later, addresses attack vectors that were left unpatched and also lets attackers hijack vulnerable Drupal sites. "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state," Drupal said on Wednesday. "This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised." While it has yet to share further details regarding these attacks, Drupal warned users that any unsecured website may have been compromised and advised admins to ensure the user 1 email address is one they control, and to consider resetting it. They should also check site logs for unauthorized access, focusing on unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account, and follow this guide if they find evidence the site may have been compromised. Those who can't immediately upgrade to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14 should secure the installer on all new and existing sites by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged six Drupal security flaws as being abused in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been exploited in ransomware attacks. 1pmzat.text: SAP has confirmed to BleepingComputer that it took urgent action to protect its customers after detecting suspicious activity in its IT environment. The German software giant said its evidence so far does not show downstream compromise of customer systems or data. Based in Walldorf, Germany, SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software vendors, with 110,000 employees in 157 countries, 300 million subscribers, and over $40 billion in annual revenue. Der Spiegel reported earlier today, based on an internal SAP memo it saw, that the software firm was hit by a cyberattack it tracks under the code name “Project Granite.” The software company reportedly asked all employees to keep the project details confidential. According to the German outlet, sources within the company said the attackers breached SAP’s GitHub environment, possibly with help from AI tools. Insider sources say that the attacker managed to steal authentication tokens from SAP employees and leveraged them to copy and also modify SAP source code on GitHub. BleepingComputer has contacted SAP for a statement on the reported breach, and the company acknowledged the incident and said it had taken steps to protect its customers. “SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services,” a company representative told BleepingComputer. “Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.” “Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.” SAP did not specify the environments where the suspicious activity was observed, or whether customers downloading code from its GitHub repositories or performing updates that are directly fetched or indirectly fed by those repositories should take any action. BleepingComputer has asked SAP about this, but a spokesperson declined to share any further information. Meanwhile, Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) issued a public warning yesterday about agentic AI tools that empower cyberattacks, such as ARTEX, CAIRN, and PentAGI. BSI cautioned organizations in the country to focus on responding to security incidents and ensure they follow all recommended security-strengthening practices. This warning comes shortly after the national cybersecurity agencies in Switzerland and Italy reported the first detections of large-scale AI-driven cyberattacks targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector. howeil.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 27, 2026 Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a software supply chain attack that has tampered with Q-Dir and DesktopOK installation files distributed via the official SoftwareOK website. "Evidence indicates that malicious files were generated not only when users downloaded the programs directly from the official download page but also during the update process of previously installed legitimate programs," South Korean cybersecurity company AhnLab said. Q-Dir, also called the Quad Directory Explorer, is a free, lightweight file manager for Windows developed by SoftwareOK. According to its website, DesktopOK is a free Windows utility designed to save and restore desktop icon positions. The unauthorized modifications are designed such that the malicious activity is challenging to detect when running the programs, while simultaneously retrieving and deploying a Python-based remote control malware (RAT) from an external server. Once installed, the RAT payload is capable of executing shell commands and Python code, transferring files, capturing screenshots, and collecting system metadata based on commands issued by the attacker. The following product versions have been confirmed to be poisoned, given the discrepancies in the SHA-256 hashes of the installer files and the presence of additional code that triggers additional file downloads and automatic execution - Q-Dir 12.85.0.0 Q-Dir 12.84.0.0 Q-Dir 12.83.0.0 DesktopOK 12.85.0.0 DesktopOK 12.82.0.0 The exact mechanism that allowed the installation files to be replaced with a trojanized version remains unknown. "The malicious installer runs the legitimate Q-Dir or DesktopOK to lower the user's suspicion, while simultaneously downloading and installing a Python RAT package from an external server," AhnLab said. Specifically, this involves downloading two payloads from "mail.c1a2[.]top" - 7zr.exe, the legitimate 7-Zip tool to decompress files dsv2_py39_agent.7z, a package containing the RAT and Python runtime environment The attack chain is fairly straightforward in that it uses the 7-Zip tool binary to extract and run the Python RAT. The malware then sets up persistence on the host by means of a scheduled task that impersonates Microsoft Edge to fly under the radar. The task is configured to execute the RAT by launching a Python script named "py_client_dsv2.py." Upon execution, the RAT establishes communication with its command-and-control (C2) server ("8.210.69[.]51:9876") to receive tasks and run them. It supports the following features - Shell command execution Python code execution File upload and download Screenshot capture Operating system and system information It also gathers a list of running processes and compares it against an internal list of various security products used in South Korea and abroad, including AhnLab, ESTSecurity, Hauri, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Trend Micro, Avast, McAfee, ESET, Symantec, Kaspersky, Bitdefender, Sophos, Fortinet, Elastic, and Malwarebytes. Information about identified security programs is transmitted to the C2 server, so as to help the attackers better plan the next stages of the attack or serve payloads that can bypass detection. The activity has not been attributed to any known threat actor. However, AhnLab said it identified Chinese language comments in the source code, suggesting that the malware authors or attackers may have used a Chinese-speaking environment. "Users who are currently using Q-Dir or DesktopOK, or who have recently installed or updated these programs, should verify the hash values of the downloaded files and check their systems for any traces of RAT installation or execution," AhnLab said. "However, simply uninstalling and reinstalling the program may not remove a Python RAT that has already been installed. Therefore, you should also check for suspicious Python execution environments, scheduled tasks, related files, and traces of external network communication, update your antivirus engine to the latest version, and then perform a full system scan."

uzzpto.text: Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update (KB5131077). According to Microsoft, the KB5138318 out-of-band update should address stop errors with 0x139 codes triggered on affected servers when IPv6 routes expire. "Microsoft has released a new Windows out-of-band (OOB) update today, November 25, 2026, to address an issue affecting a limited number of Windows Servers with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes," it said in a message center update. "Affected devices might stop unexpectedly with stop error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE) when a route timer expires. This issue affects some Windows Server 2025 devices after installing the November 2026 Windows security hotpatch update." This emergency non-security update is now rolling out to affected Windows Server 2025 devices enrolled in hotpatch updates through Windows Update. KB5138318 will download and install automatically and will take effect without requiring IT administrators or users to restart affected devices. The November 2026 hotpatch updates are also causing issues for Windows 11 users, who are experiencing installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications, as well as printing issues on systems running Forcepoint's DLP Endpoint Agent data loss prevention solution after installing this month's hotpatch on Windows 11 systems. Windows Autopatch reached public preview in early June after an initial unveil in April 2022 and has been generally available since July 2022. Microsoft announced earlier this year, in March, that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed. One month later, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that was causing driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices in the European Union. 1vs8d0i.text: ​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges. Found by ANSSI's Jérémy Jean (who submitted a fix in August), the flaw has been dubbed NFS2ROOT by cybersecurity firm OpenSec, which shared a full remote-root exploit and a patch with the NFSD maintainers in late September. The vulnerability has existed since Linux kernel version 3.16 (released in March 2014), and it stems from a heap buffer overflow weakness in the Linux NFS server (nfsd). NFS2ROOT affects systems with a Linux kernel older than 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, or 7.4-rc1 if nfsd (v4.1 or 4.2) is loaded and running and TCP port 2049 is reachable over the Internet. Successful exploitation lets remote threat actors without privileges corrupt kernel memory and gain root access to vulnerable Linux servers exposed online through low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction. In NFS2ROOT attacks, the threat actors can exploit this flaw by sending maliciously crafted requests that cause the NFS server to write data beyond an allocated memory buffer. This lets them read kernel memory, bypass KASLR (which protects kernel memory addresses), and place a callback that can execute a command in a released memory area. When the attacker closes the NFS connection, the kernel executes the embedded command with root privileges, allowing the attacker to gain root control of the unpatched Linux server. NFS2ROOT attack flow (OpenSec) ​Although there are no reports of CVE-2026-99362 exploitation in the wild, security teams should apply the latest kernel security updates from their Linux distribution vendor immediately to block potential attacks, then reboot the system to ensure the patched kernel is in use. Those who can't apply a patch immediately should restrict access to the NFS server over TCP port 2049 to trusted clients or networks. Additionally, if NFS sharing is not required on the system, admins can stop and disable the nfs-server service in /etc/nfs.conf. "Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in," OpenSec said. "Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host." While the NFS2ROOT attacks have no network signatures, security teams can still monitor for potential signs of exploitation attempts by checking for kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server, bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source, and kernel oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames, according to OpenSec. NFS2ROOT is the latest in a long series of Linux privilege escalation security flaws disclosed and patched since the start of the year, including RefluXFS, CIFSwitch, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, PinTheft, Copy Fail, Pack2TheRoot, and DirtyDecrypt/DirtyCBC. 1cz3cdq.text: Attackers using AI agents have broken into computer systems at Swiss organizations in four of five confirmed attacks, the first such cases in the country, the country's cybersecurity agency said yesterday. Three of the attacks targeted critical infrastructure operators, and two of those succeeded, with no major disruptions reported. The victims have not been named, and it is not known who is behind the attacks. Florian Schütz, who directs Switzerland's National Cyber Security Centre, gave the figures in an interview with public broadcaster SRF. All five cases were reported in recent days. Small and medium-sized companies were among the organizations hit, and they came forward voluntarily. The agency's first notice, a security advisory published on Tuesday, said the agents had compromised the victims' IT systems in every case known at that point. Neither the notice nor yesterday's broadcast interview explains why the count changed. "These cases represent a shift in the cyber threat landscape," the advisory said. The targeted operators are in at least two sectors. Electricity, drinking water, and telecommunications suppliers are examples of what Switzerland counts as critical infrastructure, according to a news agency report on the interview. The attacks involve what the Swiss agency calls agentic offensive frameworks, AI agents that find security weaknesses and carry out attacks on their own. Its advisory named ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI as examples of agents reachable over the internet, not as the tools used in the five cases. The agents are often used to scan for known, unpatched weaknesses and can run many attacks in parallel, the agency says. When defenses respond, the agents switch methods, leaving companies significantly less time to detect an intrusion and respond. The number of AI attack tools freely reachable online has nearly doubled since October, according to the agency. The figure counts available tools, not attacks or victims. Raphael Reischuk, co-founder of Switzerland's National Test Institute for Cybersecurity, expects a larger wave of attacks and says companies underestimate the risk. Italy's national computer security incident response team, CSIRT Italia, described mass compromise campaigns in an official bulletin this week. In the cases it observed firsthand, AI-directed autonomous agents broke into a large number of systems within a few hours. The agents adapt their actions within seconds, run in parallel without human input, and chain vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials together, the bulletin says. It names ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, and DeepSeek Harness, an open-source agent whose Red Team Mode uses a built-in prompt to get past the underlying model's safety limits. Each action on its own looks like normal user or API traffic. Detection depends on context: where requests come from, how often they arrive, how much data moves, and the order in which things happen. Britain's National Cyber Security Centre reported the same pattern in agency guidance this week. "Since September 2026, the NCSC has seen a marked rise in AI-assisted cyber attacks," it said. Some incidents caused downtime on internet-facing services, and others gave attackers a foothold for further agent-driven activity. The weaknesses are old ones: credentials committed to code repositories, misconfigured infrastructure-as-code, default or missing authentication, and weaknesses in APIs. What has changed is the speed, persistence, and low cost of the attacks, the British agency says. The frameworks are also noisy, which makes them easier to detect. The European Commission has already been hit. Attackers using ARTEX broke into its human resources, medical reimbursement, and translation systems, the Commission has confirmed, in an earlier intrusion first detected on October 22. What Defenders Should Do The strongest common advice from the three agencies is to shrink the time attackers have. Their recommendations overlap: Install critical security updates on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release (Switzerland), and patch flaws already being exploited first (Italy). Disconnect or isolate internet-facing systems that cannot be patched quickly (Italy). Reduce what is reachable from the internet, using geo-blocking, allow lists, and authentication in front of services (Switzerland, UK). Require MFA or passkeys on everything reachable from the internet, and grant the lowest privileges that work (Switzerland). Watch for unusual behavior and data volumes (Switzerland), and correlate logs: agent activity shows up as bursts of requests and high error rates (UK). Put bot challenges on high-value endpoints, and use decoys such as honeytokens to catch and slow agents (UK). Load Italy's published indicator feeds into monitoring tools, noting that the indicators change quickly and are valid only for their stated timeframes (Italy).

16tq82k.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 27, 2026Zero-Day / Vulnerability Details have emerged about a new zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution. The proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, which has yet to be assigned a CVE identifier, has been tracked as 4HTTP2SHELL and 4HTTP2ROOT. "I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests," a security researcher who goes by the online alias "ek0ms savi0r" said. "No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface." The shortcoming affects Cacti Core 1.2.31, the latest version, when the guest account is enabled. It's worth noting that the guest account is disabled by default starting with Cacti version 0.8.7. At a high level, the vulnerability allows an attacker to abuse the guest access to write an unvalidated value (i.e., non-numeric text) into a setting called "preview_graphs_per_page" via "auth_profile.php?action=update_data." The configuration parameter controls how many graphs are displayed per page when viewing graphs in Preview Mode. The crafted value takes the form of arbitrary SQL strings that can be turned into a second-order SQL injection by taking advantage of the fact that Cacti does not validate that the user-provided input is actually an integer value. This, in turn, opens the door for arbitrary SQL query execution when the graph preview page ("graph_view.php") is loaded with default filters. The SQL query demonstrated by "ek0ms savi0r" is an UPDATE statement to modify a record in Cacti's poller table. In the final stage of the attack, the realtime poller endpoint ("graph_realtime.php") is invoked from the same guest session, which causes the modified row from the poller table to be read and passed as input to PHP's popen() function without any allowlist or sanitization checks. The researcher has pointed out four failures that ultimately make it possible to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution - The guest can write a numeric setting as an arbitrary string The stored default bypasses request validation Cacti's PHP PDO database driver accepts stacked statements through the SQL LIMIT clause The poller executes a database-stored command string Successful exploitation of the flaw can allow an attacker to compromise the Cacti server and provide a pivot point to the target network as it exposes sensitive data, or even suppress alerts by modifying the poller table. "Because Cacti often stores credentials and connection details for routers, switches, servers, and other devices across a network, an attacker who reaches this level of command execution can gain a foothold reaching far beyond the monitoring server itself," watchTowr said in an advisory. In the absence of a fix, users are advised to disable the guest account and restrict access to the Cacti web interface to mitigate potential risks. It's also essential to review poller configuration entries for unexpected command values and apply the fixes as soon as they become available.

112c5hw.text: French international news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP) was hit by a cyberattack Thursday, forcing it to take offline one of its main platforms for distributing news content to media organizations worldwide. The attack targeted AFP Forum, an online platform that news outlets use to browse and download the agency’s stories, photographs and videos. AFP confirmed the incident Thursday in an internal email to employees, which was quoted in the agency’s own reporting. The agency is investigating the attack with assistance from external cybersecurity experts. “AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” AFP management said in the email. “As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.” The agency is offering subscribers alternative ways to access its content while the platform remains offline, according to French media reports. AFP Forum remained inaccessible as of Friday, displaying a maintenance notice in several languages. The agency has not identified who was behind the attack or provided a timeline for restoring the service. It remains unclear whether the hackers gained access to sensitive information or whether other AFP systems were affected. The agency did not respond to a request for comment. AFP is one of the world’s three major international news agencies, alongside Reuters and the Associated Press. It traces its roots to Agence Havas, founded in 1835, and took its current name in 1944. It employs more than 1,800 journalists and has 210 bureaus worldwide. This is not the first cyberattack to disrupt the agency’s content distribution services. In September 2024, AFP detected a cyberattack on its IT systems that disrupted some of the services used to deliver news content to subscribers. The attack has not been publicly attributed to any hacking group. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

1scfpef.text: Britain’s Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said Friday that it had experienced a cyber incident, with several services taken down as a precaution. The nature of the incident has not been disclosed. In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for the DWP said the department had “taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident.” The department is the largest in the British government by spending and administers the state pension and a range of other benefits. Millions of people in the country depend on its payments for essential bills. “Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal,” the spokesperson added. The department said it was “working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible to minimise any disruption.” The incident comes days after the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it has observed “a marked rise” since September in cyberattacks assisted by artificial intelligence. Earlier this year, the British government acknowledged its yearslong approach to its own cybersecurity was flawed and warned it will be impossible to meet a previous target of securing all government organizations from known cyber vulnerabilities and attack methods by 2030. “To protect our critical national infrastructure, defend public institutions and maintain public confidence in essential public services, we must achieve a radical shift in approach and a step change in pace,” it said at the time, warning the public sector faced a “critically high” cyber risk.
