1cnz3op.text: A website can look perfectly fine to the person running it. Log out, visit the same page, and things might look different. Something similar is happening with browser extensions, where even the way you find and install one can change what it does. Checking whether software works as expected only tells you so much.Then there’s the question of who gets to use what. Stolen logins are opening doors across connected systems, while some AI servers are sitting online for anyone to use at someone else’s expense. Even software responsible for keeping the power on has found its way into an attack.Meanwhile, authorities are taking down large scam operations, extortion gangs are making comebacks, and ransomware activity is picking up. Some of the more worrying findings this week involve things most people would have little reason to suspect. The details are worth a look.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. Stolen credentials expose customer data Todoist has disclosed that an attacker gained unauthorized access to its production systems and retrieved some customer information on November 23, 2026. The incident affects 6% of its users. "Between November 22 and 23, an attacker used a stolen credential associated with our version control system to modify automated workflows in three repositories and obtain additional credentials," it said. During this time, they could also read our source code. Our investigation found no changes to application code. One of the credentials they obtained allowed them to change how employees access our internal systems. The attacker used it to take over an employee’s work account and gain access to our cloud infrastructure. On November 23, the attacker downloaded a file containing account information for some early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method. They also made targeted queries for account tokens, searched some customer content for credentials, and accessed email information through connected Todoist for Outlook accounts." Record cybersecurity acquisition CrowdStrike said it will acquire Zscaler in a deal worth $43.9 billion, making it the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record. "Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said. "The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data. With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely. We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen." Paid ads activate hidden payloads Microsoft's Edge Extensions Security Team has documented SleeperWidget, a set of over 250 extensions across Microsoft Edge Add-ons, Chrome Web Store, and Mozilla Add-ons that work as advertised unless installed through a paid search ad. Once installed that way, they collect browsing data, inject ads, and change shopping links. "Its extensions pose as maps, recipe finders, package trackers, and other everyday tools. Most deliver the features they advertise, which makes hidden behavior easier to miss," it said. "In the extensions we analyzed, installation through a paid-advertising funnel also activated browsing-data collection, ad injection, and shopping-link modification." LLMjacking without exploits An analysis of 20,354 internet-facing hosts has revealed that thousands of servers where AI services or notebook APIs have been deployed and left accessible without authentication, potentially enabling attackers to abuse them for their own purposes. "More than half of the exposed Ollama servers in this scan have already been touched by someone who is not the owner," Rapid7 said. "79% of exposed Ollama hosts list at least one :cloud model, mostly GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax and Kimi variants. An exposed, signed-in server can provide access to someone else's paid subscription, with the bill landing on the owner. This is the self-hosted version of LLMjacking, and it requires no exploit at all." Blockchain-backed malware delivery SonicWall Capture Labs has disclosed details of a Java-based loader from SilentNet, a Java-based remote access trojan and infostealer sold as a malware-as-a-service offering that's advertised on YouTube. The JAR masquerades as a mod for Minecraft Fabric and targets players who download mods from external sources. "Once loaded by the game, it pulls the player's Minecraft session token from memory. It then gets its command-and-control (C2) address from a smart contract on the Polygon blockchain, and downloads a portable Python runtime hidden inside a PNG image to run a second-stage infostealer," SoniWall said. "Every string in the JAR is hidden by per-character arithmetic; it resolves hostnames through DNS-over-HTTPS, and it talks to its C2 through a custom HTTPS client that skips certificate validation." AI-powered phishing infrastructure Threat actors are using DeepSite, Hugging Face's AI website builder, to create dozens of phishing and credential-stealing pages on Hugging Face Spaces impersonating 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase, and Coinbase. "29 of the pages were built with DeepSite, Hugging Face’s AI website builder," Aikido said. "One Microsoft login clone took about 90 minutes of plain-language prompts, and other operators asked the builder to hide their pages from crawlers or send stolen logins to Telegram." Credential theft spans 127 CVEs According to VulnCheck, requests to steal credentials made up 13% of all vulnerability exploitation recorded between January and November 2026. Credential-harvesting attempts appeared across 127 of 694 CVEs observed in its honeypot network, with open-source software and AI developer tools like Apache, Laravel, Langflow, Flowise, MLflow, and n8n taking up 61% of the CVEs associated with credential-harvesting attempts. "Attackers search application files, logs and environment variables for database passwords, cloud credentials and API keys, with file-read and SSRF vulnerabilities providing opportunities without code execution," VulnCheck said, adding it "observed 1,756 attempts targeting AI provider and coding agent credentials from 406 IP addresses across 27 CVEs." Ransomware disrupts critical services A previously unknown ransomware and data-extortion group calling itself BYOD has claimed at least nine organizations between October 5 and November 9, 2026. "Its attacks have had real-world consequences, including ambulance diversion, more than 30 clinics closed, and campus-wide device shutdowns," TrendAI said. "BYOD runs a pressure campaign alongside the intrusion: audio messages on infected computers, public leak-site posts, statements framing its attacks as holding organizations accountable, and outreach to individual victims." Although the complete intrusion chain remains to be analyzed, evidence points to credential compromise and a remote access trojan on an employee's computer for initial access. Malicious JavaScript delivery platform A malware campaign has been observed installing a fake WordPress plugin built almost entirely by a name generator, including its title, directories, files, and functions (e.g., trijavascriptly, ultravueal, maxdataic, and quadmicroservicesion). "Behind the generated names is a second-stage delivery platform that runs arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of every anonymous visitor to an infected site, routes that traffic through the victim's own domain, and lies dormant for logged-in users," Wordfence said. The malware has been discovered twice, once in January 2026 and another in September 2026. Exactly how the plugin is installed is not known, but investigation shows that it's likely via a compromise of an administrator account. Global scam networks disrupted The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced that over 17.3 million scam accounts have been deplatformed on Meta, 700 fraudulent crypto investment websites seized, and 12 U.S. arrest warrants issued as part of efforts to tackle foreign and domestic scams over the past six months. The Strike Force has traced and restrained $1,082,260,156.82 in cryptocurrency stolen from U.S. victims. "Our Scam Center Strike Force has continued its work investigating cyber-enabled fraud perpetrated against Americans by transnational organized crime groups, emanating out of Asia and attacking America's main street," said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. "The Strike Force teams focus on identifying and pursuing key leaders — including Chinese organized crime affiliates operating in Cambodia, Laos, and Burma, and rapidly expanding around the globe — to bring them to justice." FBI Director Kash Patel said the Operation Blackout scam demolition initiative has "seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 digital devices, directly warned over 11,000 Americans from scam attempts, and prevented more than $690 million in potential victim losses." Over 29 scam compounds operating across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East have been dismantled and more than 2,200 trafficked workers have been repatriated. The U.S. State Department has also worked with U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to facilitate the freezing of more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, the takedown of over 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts, and several arrests. Earlier this month, the U.S. Attorney's Office also filed a civil forfeiture action to recover 456,602 USDT (Tether) that's alleged to be proceeds of romance fraud schemes targeting individuals in Massachusetts and elsewhere on online dating sites and Facebook. Billion-dollar crypto recovery bid The Justice Department has filed a civil action to recover over $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency that was illicitly obtained from Binance by North Korean actors in a major hack last month. "To date, the United States has assisted in the freezing, seizing, and/or the return of almost $3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from multiple sources since the theft from Binance on or about October 29," the DoJ said. Brett Leatherman, Cyber Branch Operations Director of the FBI, said, "North Korea depends on sophisticated laundering techniques to convert stolen cryptocurrency into funds that support the regime's illicit activities," adding, "Following the Binance theft, the FBI and our partners moved quickly to trace and freeze stolen assets and share critical information with virtual asset service providers." Extortion gang resurfaces after arrests The ShinyHunters extortion gang claims to have returned on a new data leak site following a series of arrests targeting alleged members. The new TOR site, launched on November 23, features messages in both Russian and English announcing the group's return, while denouncing a former member, Rey (aka Saif), who was reportedly arrested and is "actively cooperating" with law enforcement. "We want to let you know that from now on we will only be using our account on Exploit, which we've held since 2020," the group said. "We won't be active on any other BF-style forums anymore." They also concluded the statement with a shout-out to two other arrested members, Umbreon and Ed Dubrovsky. "Thank you for being with us all this time," the group said. "We won't forget you, and we might even send you a couple of postcards to your rat-infested cells. It was a pleasure working with you. And it's truly a shame that our guys got caught because of such silly mistakes, ones that could easily have been avoided if you fools hadn't gotten involved with the wrong people." AI misuse detection without data retention Anthropic has launched a public beta of Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), allowing organizations to detect potentially harmful AI activity across multiple interactions while maintaining zero data retention (ZDR). The protection employs a second defensive layer, known as automated safety monitoring, that looks for patterns of misuse across multiple requests to provide automated safety monitoring without storing any customer data. "Instead, our automated safety monitoring system analyzes data stored entirely on infrastructure controlled by our customers," Anthropic said. "When automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for you to review. These cases can be read from your cloud storage or through an API, and can be integrated with security information and event management systems. They do not include inputs and outputs. Once it's set up, automated safety monitoring can help your team detect intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm (like offensive cyber operations). It can also help detect agents that take actions beyond a user's intentions." Ransomware activity jumps 23% NCC Group has revealed that ransomware attacks surged 23% in October 2026 compared to September, with 1049 claimed incidents. The Gentlemen, N0n, Qilin, Akira, and Silent Ransom have claimed the most victims. Top targeted verticals included industrials, consumer discretionary, healthcare, IT, and consumer supplies. Check Point Research has reported a record 2,830 ransomware victims in Q3 2026, claimed by 117 ransomware brands, up from 91 in the previous quarter. Of these, 42 are new. "Ransom payments continued to diverge: average payments fell 45% quarter over quarter to just over $1 million, while the median rose 167% to $400,000," Check Point said. "The top 10 groups accounted for just 49% of victims, the first time groups outside the top ten collectively represented the majority." Qilin, The Gentlemen, and INC Ransom emerged as the most active groups during the period. Interestingly, while the top 10 groups accounted for 71% of victims in Q1 2026, the figure has declined to 58% in Q2 and only 49% in Q3, indicating a fragmentation of the threat landscape. 12,200 online stores compromised A new analysis from Guardio Labs has revealed that one online shop in 195 (i.e., about 12,200 of the 2.38 million stores) was hijacked in October 2026. The phenomenon has been codenamed CartJacked. "Three schemes go straight after shoppers: hand-offs to gambling and scam pages, fake 'I'm not a robot' checks that tell you to paste a command (about 900 shops), and card skimmers," Guardio said. "Of the ten commands the fake checks handed out, three still delivered malware, including a stealer for passwords and crypto wallets." €26 million crypto trail uncovered A Europol-led operation along with authorities from 11 countries has disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services and the identification of 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content as part of a five-day effort between November 16 and 20, 2026. The sites drew over 7.3 million visits each year. More than €26 million in cryptocurrency transactions have been traced so far. "The operation targeted a criminal market worth billions of euros annually, in which illegal streaming providers sell unauthorized access to premium television channels, live sports and films, often collecting subscription payments through cryptocurrency," Europol said. "The profits generated by these services do not simply disappear. They move through payment accounts, cryptocurrency wallets and intermediaries, making it harder for investigators to identify who is ultimately benefiting." No arrests have been announced. 10 million exposed NGINX services at risk Censys has revealed that more than 10 million exposed NGINX services are running an affected version with HTTP/2 that are vulnerable to a set of flaws called NGINX2Root that "could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to corrupt memory in an NGINX worker process when a set of specific features are enabled – leading to code execution where ASLR is disabled or the attacker can bypass it." Power management software weaponized Broadcom-owned Symantec has disclosed details of an intrusion in which the attacker used CyberPower PowerPanel Business (PPB), a software that manages UPS devices, as a way to execute code on a domain controller, dump Active Directory secrets and launch a persistent implant. "PPB can run a script (a .cmd file in an extcmd folder) when a power-related event such as a voltage sag or outage is detected," Symantec said. "The attacker placed their own scripts in that folder through the product's web console and had the PowerPanel service, ppbed.exe, run them. The commands in this attack chain have ppbed.exe as their ancestor and run as SYSTEM. The attacker used this channel to download tools with certutil, then loaded a .NET assembly into memory using PowerShell, and ran ntdsutil and esentutl against the Active Directory database, ntds.dit." The same channel has also been used to launch an implant ("upnpcont.exe") that uses DLL sideloading to launch a suspicious DLL ("atl.dll"). "What this attack shows is that UPS, power-management, and other infrastructure software should be treated like any other potentially dual-use RMM product; used with network restrictions, unique credentials, vigilant patching, and process-level monitoring," Symantec said. Banking middleware weaponized A new campaign called BankWeaver has targeted a Temenos Quantum Fabric deployment with an exposed authentication service that was configured to accept anonymous access to obtain administrator privileges and deliver malicious Java components via the platform's extension mechanism. The attack targeted an unspecified financial services institution in early September 2026. "Attackers could generate an anonymous token by accessing a public application and then exchange it for an administrator token on another exposed application," Forescout said. "The new token obtained by the attackers granted access to administrative functions within the Temenos Fabric platform, including managing running applications and creating new services." The malicious components delivered as part of the attack include: FabricShell, which provides arbitrary command execution and database queries, and FabricShadow, which collects host information, stages output locally, and exfiltrates results to remote servers. Temenos has since released updates and guidance to configure the service as private and advised customers to restrict internet access to Spotlight and Fabric administrative and authentication services. Fake updates deliver Python backdoor A new wave of Microsoft Teams social engineering activity exhibiting similarities to Edgecution was uncovered by Arctic Wolf Labs last month. "In the October wave, following a lull in observed cases from August to September, new delivery artifacts and operational patterns were observed," the cybersecurity company said. "The campaign abuses a malicious Edge extension and Chrome Native Messaging to run a Python backdoor outside the browser sandbox. The activity shares early chain tradecraft with PREY-0059, including external-tenant Teams impersonation of IT support, legitimate runtimes paired with scripts, and S3-hosted payloads disguised as legitimate software. While PREY-0059 used S3 buckets named after targeted victims and delivered a Java-based RAT alongside a Java runtime, the current activity used generic Microsoft-themed tenants and buckets, an Edge extension, and a Python backdoor paired with a Python runtime." One thing worth taking away from this week's stories is how much damage can happen without a particularly clever attack. A forgotten server, a stolen credential, or a feature nobody thought to monitor can be enough. AI may be changing how some attacks are carried out, but many of the ways attackers get in are still surprisingly ordinary.The harder part is knowing what deserves attention before it becomes a problem. That includes software sitting quietly in the background, services exposed for convenience, and accounts with more access than they need. […]

yoxj54.text: An ongoing phishing campaign dubbed "GoodGuys" impersonates major brands, including Google, Nvidia, Accenture, and SpaceX, to steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars. The attacks offer recipients up to $600 for a 45-minute interview in an attempt to get them to sign in with their work accounts to participate. The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American Express, Coca-Cola, Culver's, Google Cloud, Nvidia, SpaceX, and Spotify. The threat actors abuse legitimate email and event platforms, including HireVue, SendGrid, Mandrill, and Cvent, to distribute phishing links. In one attack, a phishing email sent through HireVue invited recipients to attend a Google Cloud webinar about deploying AI applications into production. Phishing email impersonating Google Cloud Source: Push Security The threat actors use domains themed around interviews, webinars, and research studies, creating brand-specific subdomains to host the phishing pages, such as: accenture[.]international-interviews[.]com nvidia[.]feedback-study[.]com google[.]webinar-cloud[.]com spotify[.]interview-experts[.]com Clicking the phishing links typically takes recipients to a CAPTCHA challenge before displaying a website impersonating the company that supposedly sent the invitation. Each website features customized branding and lures, with the Nvidia phishing site offering $500 to participate in an AI feedback study and the Accenture site offering $600 for an expert interview. The sites ultimately prompt visitors to sign in with their Google accounts to validate their invitations, allowing the attackers to steal their credentials. The phishing kit specifically targets corporate accounts and rejects email addresses associated with Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook. Unlike adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits that use reverse proxies to relay legitimate login pages, GoodGuys uses fake authentication forms controlled by an attacker-controlled server. After victims enter their Google credentials, the phishing page can display various multifactor authentication (MFA) challenges, including requests for SMS codes, authenticator codes, and Google sign-in prompts requiring users to select a matching number on their phones. The kit also includes fake Okta authentication forms and support for Okta Verify push notifications. Push Security believes the threat actors manually attempt to log in using the stolen credentials, instructing the phishing page to display whatever MFA or security challenges Google or Okta show during authentication. Similar techniques were used in vishing-based data theft attacks linked to the ShinyHunters extortion gang earlier this year to steal corporate single sign-on (SSO) credentials. Suspected GoodGuys credential and MFA relay attack Source: Push Security Once the process is completed, the phishing kit redirects victims to another website or displays a message thanking them for their application. The researchers believe the phishing kit may have been developed using an AI coding assistant, based on hidden accessibility labels found in every analyzed version of the kit. "The sign-in card in every build carries two hidden labels: "Sign-in simulation" and "GoodGuys sign-in simulation." They sit in accessibility text that only screen readers announce, so a visitor never sees them. We think the label is a leftover from how the kit was first built," explained Push Security. "Calling the page a sign-in "simulation" for a made-up company is the kind of framing someone would use to get an AI coding assistant past its guardrails when asking it to build a phishing page. The label then stayed in every build we've collected." The researchers also discovered a potentially related phishing campaign that uses fake Coca-Cola interview invitations and the Evilginx phishing kit to target Google Ads accounts. While both campaigns used the same abused SendGrid click tracker and identical Coca-Cola branding assets, differences in their code and infrastructure prevented researchers from conclusively linking the attacks to the same threat actor. 1qc0w3v.text: The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's email service. On November 8, the Remus infostealer developer started advertising the alleged Gmail zero-day flaw that allowed the malware to collect emails even if victims changed their passwords and revoked all sessions. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock investigated the claims but came to inconclusive results. The researchers noted that evidence from the malware customers matched the seller's pitch, although there was no technical proof that a zero-day vulnerability was being exploited. Remus stealer panel Source: GenDigital GenDigital and Invoke RE researchers published their independent findings yesterday, explaining that the advertised “zero-day” was just a malicious Chrome extension installed on the victims' browsers. The extension is designed to steal unread emails from signed-in Gmail accounts. It can also survive password changes and session revocations because it remains installed in the victim's Chrome browser. Its access to Gmail stops when the active session ends, and resumes again when the victim signs back in. GenDigital discovered the extension after reverse-engineering the Remus infostealer. The researchers found no trace of an email-stealing module, suggesting that the functionality is implemented via an add-on. “In a nutshell, the loaded module is a native DLL whose sole purpose is to install a malicious extension into Google Chrome, which, notably, is the only browser it targets,” GenDigital explains. “The extension itself is bundled directly inside the DLL, stored as an unencrypted ZIP archive in its .rdata section.” GenDigital explains that Chrome versions 137 and later removed a command-line option that allowed malware to load extensions. Remus takes a complex route to overcome this restriction, editing the victim’s Chrome profile to register the malicious extension and then enabling ‘Developer Mode’ in the browser, which is required to run unpacked extensions. The extension uses the name “Google Sheets,” copies the description of Google Docs Offline, and requests access to all websites. Installed malicious extension Source: GenDigital Once active in the browser, it checks for unread emails every minute across up to 10 account slots and retrieves them in full, in raw format. The extension sends the email subject, message body, sender, and victim’s email address to its command-and-control server, along with a campaign identifier. Email theft Source: GenDigital Failed uploads are queued and retried, while a local record helps the extension keep track of what has succeeded so it doesn’t send duplicates. Although the extension also parses attachment filenames, it does not send those to its operators, so this feature may not be fully implemented yet. To defend against this threat, users are advised to download software only from trusted sources and scrutinize “chrome://extensions” for rogue installations or unexpected activation of Developer Mode. 1eup45s.text: The threat actors behind the PolinRider campaign have been observed planting a Python loader in GitHub repositories, as evidence emerges that the activity may have started as far back as February 2025. "The loader hides in a small utils package or in conftest.py," SafeDep said in a report published this week. "When Python imports the file, the loader reads the newest transaction that an Ethereum wallet sent to itself. It decodes the input data of that transaction as JavaScript and runs it with Node.js." The JavaScript code, for its part, reads a second wallet to locate the command-and-control (C2) server and then passes the next stage to a detached interactive Node.js environment by means of a node -i process. The software supply chain security company said it identified the loader in 375 public repositories that belong to 260 accounts. There is no evidence that the loader has been distributed via PyPI or npm. PolinRider is the name assigned to a malicious campaign linked to North Korean threat actors. Recent reports indicate that the activity employs various channels to distribute malware, including - Fraudulent recruitment campaigns that make use of phishing emails and fake hiring portals like BlockNovas, AccuraSoftHire ("accurasofthire[.]com") and HuntRole ("huntrole[.]org") to trick prospective targets into running malware-laced projects under the pretext of a take-home assessment. Publishing malicious packages across open-source ecosystems by hijacking maintainer accounts to plant obfuscated malware through fake font files (fa-solid-400.woff2, fa-solid-500.woff2, or fa-solid-300.llf), Visual Studio Code (VS Code) auto-run tasks, and Git history rewriting. Using compromised developer machines to steal their GitHub tokens and force-push malicious commits into open-source repositories they have access to. At a high level, the PolinRider loader retrieves an encrypted second-stage Node.js payload that scans the infected host for installed developer applications, such as GitHub Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and Google Antigravity, and tampers with the most frequently used tools to execute attacker-controlled code and deliver infostealer malware. It's worth noting here that PolinRider is assessed to be a sub-cluster operating in parallel with a long-running campaign codenamed Contagious Interview. While the latter is more of a social-engineering entry point that's used to compromise developer systems, PolinRider abuses the access to modify repositories and turn them into a distribution channel for malware. "Cybercriminal groups deploy supply chain worms for opportunistic theft. On the other hand, North Korean state-sponsored threat actors use open-source software registries as a primary initial access vector targeting corporate environments," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said in a report published last month. "Threat actors demonstrate how compromising a single maintainer account or registry scope converts open-source dependencies, resulting in widespread affected cloud environments." Some of the decoy sites have been found to incorporate two other alternate delivery paths - Instruct candidates to sideload a Google Chrome extension after enabling "Developer mode" to subscribe to new job alerts. Employ ClickFix-style lures to get victims to copy and paste malicious commands into the terminal app depending on the operating system as part of a "standard settings bundle for candidates and interview workflows." "The [job] application asks for a short verification video," StepSecurity said. "Until the server marks a candidate as having installed a 'driver,' the camera check always fails with a message saying the system does not have a compatible camera environment." "A separate 'Technical onboarding' page on the site gives a one-line curl command to download the 'driver.' On Windows, the downloaded installer fetches a script from the careers site that installs Node.js if it is missing, downloads a JavaScript payload, runs it in the background and deletes itself. The macOS and Linux versions do the same." The JavaScript malware is designed to perform the following steps - Read the latest transaction associated with an Ethereum wallet ("0xa322E5f3D311D3080e6f0121063e9aDC2490Ef1a"). Get its destination wallet address ("0x67B38e9b67B38E9b68656c6C6f6970626f742121"). Extract the C2 server address twice ("103.179.142[.]155") from the first eight bytes ("67B38e9b" and "67B38E9b") of the wallet address, using a technique referred to as NullReceiver, while the last 12 bytes represent the ASCII string "helloipbot!!." Use the IP address to fetch two payloads, "0x/cls" and "0x/ls," over port 443. The NullReceiver technique The latest findings from SafeDep show that the repositories are injected with a 58-line Python loader that reads the "0x3b1574417524c11a7403c4b232CAcBb320CceBC6" wallet to extract JavaScript code that then reaches out to a second wallet ("0x1eEf0849EDa15d87f64e51C73C8442Cf3c8bCEF3") to obtain the destination wallet associated with the latest transaction ("0x5F87b5545F87b55468656C6C6f6970626f742121"), which is then used to parse the C2 server ("95.135.181[.]84"). A defining aspect of NullReceiver is the marker "68656c6C6f6970626f742121" in the made-up destination wallet address that consistently translates to "helloipbot!!." "The /0x/cls script runs twice, once with eval in the current process and once in a new process," SafeDep said. "The /0x/ls script runs only in a new process." The exact nature of these payloads remains unknown. However, prior waves have been observed installing a stealer that harvests environment secrets, browser passwords, cookies, and wallet data. Interestingly, the wallet address "0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3" has been reused by the threat actors across other attack waves - Pushing compromised versions of legitimate npm packages such as @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/health-api-server, @adminide-stack/user-activity-browser, @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/forms-core, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser, server-hemera-mongo, cdeops, @cdmbase/wiki-browser, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser that use the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]151." A fake recruitment campaign from HuntRole that convinces victims to complete a coding assessment, which uses a VS Code extension named "huntrole.assessment-tool" from the Visual Studio Marketplace to send system information and fetch and run a malicious JavaScript payload. The script queries the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84." Using a GitHub account named " Eternity0207 " to open over 200 pull requests targeting open-source projects like AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse, and Open Food Facts, and subsequently force-push a modified commit containing an obfuscated loader that uses the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84." According to the maintainer of AsyncAPI Generator, "Each time, the payload stayed on the branch for 30-40 minutes and was then force-pushed away, so the final diff looked clean." The unauthorized modifications allowed the loader to run when an unsuspecting developer runs "npm run build" (for AsyncAPI), loads the test configuration (for Open Food Facts), or opens the folder in VS Code (for CircuitVerse). The GitHub account has since been suspended. According to estimates from Apiiro, PolinRider has been detected in at least 7,609 GitHub repos owned by 2,330 accounts, most of them belonging to developers. Some of the victims include Neutralinojs, InstaWP Connect, and fxhash. The loader has been pushed to 2,040 repositories between October 27 and November 6, 2026. "The worm uses stolen GitHub access to rewrite commits the developer already made, keeping the author, message and date, and adds a loader hidden after hundreds of spaces in a build config," Apiiro researcher Shmulik Cohen said. "Building the project runs it. In the newest wave, opening the folder in VS Code is enough. The loader reads its server from an Ethereum wallet, so taking a server down changes nothing: one transaction moves every loader to the next." PolinRider attack from May 2025 The development comes as OpenSourceMalware said it discovered a PolinRider attack from May 2025, predating the earliest documented victims by eight months. The attack targeted nine packages, using hijacked maintainer account to push poisoned versions within a span of 90 minutes - itsa-utils@1.4.2 itsa-jsext@2.0.3 itsa-react-docviewer@16.1.2 itsa-cli@16.5.3 itsa-react-button@16.0.11 itsa-react-maskedinput@16.1.2 itsa-react-checkbox@16.0.5 itsa-react-focuscontainer@16.0.10 itsa-react-input@16.1.2 Each of these packages have been found to leverage EtherHiding, a precursor to NullReceiver, to retrieve a JavaScript downloader called JADESNOW, which is then used to deliver InvisibleFerret, a Python-based backdoor used in Contagious Interview campaigns, along with a Socket.IO RAT and a Python-based stealer. "The 2025 sample carries PolinRider's payload but not its documented spread behavior, which appears in the same maintainer's GitHub repositories in four windows between January and July 2026," security researchers Paul McCarty and Jenn Gile said. "The blockchain records behind it date attacker activity back to February 2025." "The infection likely persisted on the maintainer's machine from 2025, because the 2026 pushes ran from it. That matches PolinRider's documented propagation script, which rolls back the clock, folds the payload into the tip commit, and force-pushes with the developer's own credentials."

151milj.text: Every phishing attack has to get past email security, web filtering, and safe browsing before it reaches an employee. Some kits manage that far more often than others, and those are the kits that security teams need to know about. At Push Security, we measure this as breakthrough rate: The share of attacks that get past email security, web gateways, and safe browsing to reach the user. How an attack breaks through Every browser-based attack starts with a lure, and each control in its path sees only part of the attack: Email security: Half of the attacks we see never touch email. The lure arrives through a search ad, a chat message, social media, a calendar invite, or a QR code. The rest come from trusted senders and services, so they pass reputation checks. Web gateways: The pages sit on trusted hosting and are assembled in the browser. The domains rotate every few days, so reputation data lags behind them. Safe browsing and scanners: Bot checks and cloaking show scanners a harmless page. A new domain isn't on any blocklist yet. How a phishing attack gets past email, URL, DNS, web gateway, and scanner controls before it reaches the user in the browser. When the page loads in the user's browser and the user interacts with it, that's a breakthrough. Breakthrough rate counts those attacks, not attempts. This changes how to read upstream data. A kit with a high breakthrough rate is one that upstream controls are missing. A low count in email or proxy logs doesn't prove that a kit is rare, because the kit may be getting past those controls without a trace. Our upcoming webinar reveals the five kits with the highest breakthrough rates. Here's an early look at the number one kit. Save your spot for the webinar DOMDIFFER: Google's real sign-in page, mirrored from the attacker's browser From August to October 2026, one kit ranked first by breakthrough rate every month. DOMDIFFER, an AiTM phishing kit that targets corporate Google and Microsoft accounts, broke through 2-4x as often as the next kit each month. DOM mirroring, the mechanism it uses under the hood, also happens to be the newest and fastest-growing way for a kit to relay a sign-in. We first saw DOMDIFFER in February 2026. DOMDIFFER is our name for the kit (it hasn't yet been linked to a known phishing-as-a-service brand). We believe it grew out of NakedPages, a reverse proxy kit, and the two kits share infrastructure in several places. DOMDIFFER went quiet in the spring, came back over the summer, and has held the top rating since August. Most of its detections in that time came from fake calendar event lures. New hostnames per month for three NakedPages variants and DOMDIFFER, from our threat intelligence. One real DOMDIFFER attack starts with a fake Google Voice notification about a new voicemail. The lure for one DOMDIFFER attack: A fake Google Voice voicemail notification. The link passes a bot check that turns scanners away. The victim then sees what looks exactly like Google's sign-in page. It isn't a screenshot or a static copy. It's Google's real page, mirrored from the attacker's browser. Google's sign-in page, mirrored from the attacker's browser by DOMDIFFER. On the surface, this looks like fairly standard phishing: A notification lure, a bot check gate, then a sign-in page. What makes DOMDIFFER particularly effective lies beneath the surface. TL;DR: DOM mirroring AiTM kits relay a sign-in in one of four ways: Reverse proxy, replica page, pixel streaming, and DOM mirroring. In DOM mirroring, the attacker's own browser does the real sign-in. It sends the page's structure (the DOM) to the victim's browser, which rebuilds a working copy. Because a real browser does the sign-in, the kit sends Google genuine browser signals and handles new sign-in steps without needing extra code. Replica pages are still the most common class, but DOM mirroring is the newest and the fastest growing in 2026. Laurseraph, the main criminal pixel-streaming kit, has switched to DOM mirroring, and kits such as BlueKit and PhantomDOM use it too. How common each AiTM class is today, with example kits for each. What the victim's browser gets in each AiTM class, and what relays the sign-in. Orange lines mark an attacker's browser in the middle. Our research post, From reverse proxies to DOM mirroring, explains the four classes in detail. Under the hood DOM mirroring is only part of why DOMDIFFER breaks through security controls. The rest comes from how the kit reaches its victims and stays out of sight of the controls along the way. In the webinar on December 2, Luke will take apart DOMDIFFER and the other four kits in the top five. He'll show how each one works under the hood, and the tricks that get them past controls more often than other kits. Why controls fall short Passkeys are worth rolling out, and they stop AiTM phishing where they're enforced. But AiTM is now one payload among several, and attackers are getting creative with how they combine them. Kits use AiTM interchangeably with payloads that passkeys don't touch. In authorization attacks such as device code phishing, the victim signs in on Microsoft's real page and grants the attacker access. Other kits skip the sign-in page altogether and trick the victim into installing a remote access tool instead. Kits pick the payload to match the visitor. A Windows visitor might get a remote access tool, a Microsoft account device code phishing, and a Google account AiTM. Some lures now carry two kits at once, so closing one path leaves another open. Each of these gaps ends the same way: A page loads in the browser, and a user acts on it. In the webinar, Luke will show attackers use these tricks in real attacks. What the webinar reveals DOMDIFFER is one of five kits that broke through most often from August to October. On December 2, Luke Jennings will reveal the other four in a live threat briefing. Join the webinar to see: The other four kits in the top five, and the techniques behind each one How DOMDIFFER works under the hood, and the tricks that get it past controls Real attacks from the top kits, from the lure to the stolen session How kits now choose the payload to match the visitor's platform Which techniques and kits should be on your radar heading into 2027 If you can't make it, register anyway and you'll get a copy of the recording. Register for the webinar now.

1j4aj6k.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 26, 2026Data Breach / Password Security Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. "While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said. It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts. As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure. According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including - Names Email addresses Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times Public keys Secure Remote Password protocol parameters Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers 1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified. "The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security." "Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."

1489tuw.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 26, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states that could still be abused to facilitate site takeover even after the fix. CVE-2026-132165 "recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer," Drupal maintainers said. "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites." "It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state." Drupal acknowledged that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, but emphasized that site owners who have already secured the installer ("install.php") are not impacted. Specifically, any website that left its installer remotely accessible following the fix for CVE-2026-132165 may have been compromised. Drupal is urging site administrators to take the following actions - Check site logs for unauthorized access, including unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account Ensure the user 1 email address is set to under their control, and consider resetting user 1's password. The issue has been remediated in the following versions - Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.14 Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.23 Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.23 Drupal 11.0.x to 11.2.x - No fix (End-of-life) Drupal 10.5.x and below - No fix (End-of-life) After updating to the latest supported versions, it's recommended to run "update.php" to fix existing production sites in this state and secure the Drupal installer on all new and existing sites. According to statistics shared by StepSecurity, there are about 55,800 internet-facing Drupal sites as of November 26, 2026, out of which 31,500 services are running branches that are vulnerable to CVE-2026-132165 and roughly 15,000 are on the end-of-life 8 and 9 branches.

mlxv45.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 26, 2026Industrial Control Systems / Vulnerability The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added 10 security flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including five vulnerabilities impacting Mitel MiCollab that were disclosed last week. The Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An arbitrary file upload vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to upload arbitrary files to the target system. CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score: 9.0) - An XML injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score: 5.9) - An unauthorized access vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information. CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score: 10.0) - A command injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An authentication bypass vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication controls and perform unauthorized actions within the context of the application. The issues affect MiCollab versions 10.3 and earlier. "Mitel provided a patch available for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) that addresses these vulnerabilities," the company said in an advisory published November 16, 2026. "Upgrade to this release and apply the provided patch, or upgrade to a later release." Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. As of writing, there are currently no details on how the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild. Also added to the KEV catalog are the following vulnerabilities - CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper validation of specified type of input vulnerability in Vates Xen Orchestra that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and perform actions with administrative privileges via a specially crafted authentication token containing an empty JSON object. CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID. The addition of CVE-2026-133469 follows an advisory from Vates VMS that the vulnerability, also tracked as VSA-2026-062, has been exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain - 91.211.251[.]112:8001 ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333 "At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT," Juniper Networks said in an advisory. "Customers are encouraged to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime take steps to mitigate this vulnerability." The remaining three security flaws relate to Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series refrigeration controllers that could lead to authentication bypass and arbitrary command execution - CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an attacker to access and read underlying server system files via the XML interface. CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on the affected system. CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authentication vulnerability that could allow an attacker to generate a web report exposing sensitive information, including internal IP addresses, usernames, and store names. Although Danfoss makes no mention of the flaws being exploited, it's likely that they were put to use as part of high-impact attacks targeting supermarket chains across Europe in recent weeks. France has attributed the October 2026 attacks on its retail sites to Shahid Kaveh (aka Cyber Aveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front), an Iranian cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are being advised to apply the necessary fixes for all the flaws, except CVE-2026-133311 and CVE-2025-41450, by November 28, 2026. The remaining two vulnerabilities must be addressed by December 9, 2026.CISA Warns of New Unpatched Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series Flaw The development comes as CISA has warned of an unpatched critical flaw in Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series (CVE-2026-129713, CVSS score: 9.8 / 9.3) controllers that could be exploited to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges. "A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges," CISA said. "Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability." Danfoss, which has issued an alert of its own, said the security flaw impacts versions 5.4.0 and earlier. A fix for the vulnerability is expected to be addressed in an upcoming software version (5.5.x). It also said it will remove the option that allows customers to disable "Strict mode" in the product. Until the fixes are available, system administrators are advised to take the following actions - Make sure remote access to the units is possible only through a secure VPN or in general over a protected network Configure the units to Strict mode, which ensures higher security levels on the product Recommend using strong passwords CISA is also recommending that organizations minimize network exposure of such devices, place control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls, and isolate them from business networks. "When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available," CISA added. "Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices."

jnd4c2.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows .NET developers under the guise of a fake take-home job assessment. "Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF [Windows Presentation Foundation] button controls," Socket security researcher Kush Pandya said in a technical write-up. "In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL sideloading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable." All the identified NuGet packages have been deleted from the gallery as of writing. The names of the packages are listed below - WinUI.Button VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer HappyOne.WinUI3Controls Web3TotalButton RevertButtonIcon WinUI3IconButton WindowsAccentColorName SetButtonColor InitializeCustomButton StyledAppButton StyledComponent The first NuGet package, WinUI3IconButton, was uploaded to the registry on July 23, 2026, indicating that the campaign has been ongoing for quite some time without attracting attention. The last two uploads, HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls, occurred on November 4, 2026, after both VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls were removed by NuGet on November 2, 2026. The starting point is a GitHub repository ("stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment") created on November 3, 2026. It features a set of assessment tasks revolving around enhancing a FileButton control and exception handling that candidates must implement within a span of three to four hours. It's unclear how targets are led to these decoy projects. The README file also permits the test participants to use artificial intelligence (AI) development assistants like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude, but discourages them from copying and pasting the entire project into the tool and generating the solution without "understanding it." Present within the assessment repository is a "WinUI3_Home_Assessment.csproj" file that references VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer version 1.2.7 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls version 1.0.7. "VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL ['MSBuildAnalyzer.dll'] after every build," Pandya said. "In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it." The VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package then launches the copied binary via the FileButton control that "routes clicks to Windows files and folders," triggering the execution of the DLL via a known technique called DLL sideloading. In a similar vein, creating a WUIButton control from the WinUI.Button package starts a background routine in "lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll" that downloads "avast.exe" from the "Carol-White-Super/cloud" repository via the GitHub API using an embedded access token, saves it as "%TEMP%\Launcher.exe," and runs it. RevertButtonIcon and SetButtonColor "download a Windows executable to the user's temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops," Socket explained. "Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to." Socket also said it identified two bogus repositories impersonating the axios JavaScript library - jason-code-super/axios stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (the same GitHub account hosting the assessment) Both repositories have been flagged as copies of a malicious Node.js library named "axios-test-one" that impersonates the Axios HTTP client but contains functionality that enables code execution and shell access. The repositories serve a Windows executable named "lib/env/axios.csproj." An analysis of their commit history has revealed several binaries between the two repositories, including - A loader ("updater.exe" and "msedgewebview2.exe") that uses a GitHub repository ("James-White-Super/React_prj") as a two-way command and control (C2) A PyInstaller program that functions as a Google Chrome profile stealer and uploads the information to GitHub ("gabsantosbus-star/EngineeringRepository"), and A "WeapF" payload that reports the computer name, user name, time zone, and CPU model to an attacker-controlled Telegram bot What's more, the GitHub account named "gabsantosbus-star" (aka Gabriel) has been found to have made the first commit in the two aforementioned fake Axios repositories, along with "figma-share/axios-http," a third bogus Axios repository. "On November 13, 2026, gabsantosbus-star [...] published a GitHub release of 'Crypto Wallet Analyzer,' a single-file .NET app," Socket said. "The README presents the app as a first-stage client deliverable that inventories eight crypto wallet extensions in Chrome profiles and makes no network requests." "The visible app does only that, but its decompiled MainWindow constructor also loads a native DLL bundled in the executable. The DLL starts a background thread when loaded, and closing the window only hides it, so the process keeps running." The DLL in question is a new version of the loader that uses a different repository ("Best-Seller-Dev/dexTrader") for C2. The GitHub account is no longer accessible as of writing. Further investigation has uncovered that the lure was advertised on a Web3 freelance marketplace called LaborX on November 7, 2026, under the same persona, with the threat actor posing as a "detail-oriented client looking to work with skilled freelancers on various projects." The $8,500-10,000 job listing, which is still accessible, claims that they are looking for a C# WPF developer to work on their lightweight Windows .NET desktop application that "inventories crypto wallet software installed on a local PC, including browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications." On their X profile, they describe themselves as a "blockchain and DeFi specialist" and a "cryptocurrency expert" based out of Miami, Florida. But a check of their "About this account" reveals that the profile is actually based in Korea. The account was created in July 2026. The web of connections doesn't end there, for evidence indicates that the "axios-test-one" npm library was part of a broader collection of six packages that were published between July 14 and 23, 2026, by three npm accounts gsanbus, jasonsuperstar, and jasonsayman - axios-test-one telemetry-metrics telemetry-axios axios-native fs-extra-core vitest-axios The use of the name "jasonsayman" is particularly significant as it clearly points to an attempt to pass off as "jasonsaayman," the legitimate GitHub account belonging to the developer and maintainer of Axios. "Telemetry-metrics and telemetry-axios download a Windows executable from ThoSuperstarDev/axios-http and run it, fs-extra-core downloads one from jason-code-super/axios and saves it as msedgewebview2.exe, and the axios clones pull those packages in," Socket said. What's notable here is that "ThoSuperstarDev" is the former GitHub account name of "figma-share," which, as it happens, also hosts a ClickFix-style page that shows a fake reCAPTCHA verification prompt and guides the visitor to copy and paste a security token into the Windows Run dialog to address a purported "Security Handshake Error." The fraudulent job campaign has not been attributed to any named threat actor or group. However, Socket noted that the tradecraft shares similarities with other recruitment-themed campaigns orchestrated by North Korea and Iran. "We found no indicator or code shared with any published Contagious Interview or other North Korean campaign, none of the malware families publicly tied to Contagious Interview (such as BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, and OtterCookie) in the stages we recovered, and no publicly documented family that matches the loader," Pandya said.

cb8ztm.text: Britain has again delayed the launch of its National Cyber Action Plan, the government’s long-awaited strategy for defending the wider economy against state-backed and criminal hackers, according to multiple people familiar with the matter. The document, originally conceived as a national cyber strategy, was first due to be published by the end of 2025. After initial delays it was rebranded as an action plan and was close to publication in July this year before being postponed amid Keir Starmer’s resignation. Officials, who had planned to publish the document in mid-November, now aim to unveil it on December 9 according to several sources, speaking to Recorded Future News on condition of anonymity. The reasons for the latest delay are unclear. A government spokesperson declined to comment on the timing but said ministers remained committed to publishing the plan. The latest delay follows an influential cross-party House of Lords committee warning that the government “appears complacent” about “potentially catastrophic risks,” including cyberattacks from Russia, China and Iran. In a report published last week, the National Resilience Committee found Britain was dangerously underprepared for crises which could cascade across the economy, with disruption spilling over multiple sectors and disrupting the everyday lives of millions of people. Baroness Northover, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, told Recorded Future News that the country could not afford more uncertainty or drift. “This situation is unacceptable at a time of significant and escalating risk,” she said. “We must act urgently. The cost of inaction is enormous.” “Further absence of an overarching National Cyber Action Plan, aimed at defending the economy against state-backed and criminal hacking, is not just frustrating, it is serious,” she said. “The UK has got to keep pace with threats. Delay and avoidance is simply not an option and underlines the Committee’s point that the UK remains seriously exposed and underprepared for very significant events, and our vulnerability is current, active and acute on many fronts.” No dither but delay Successive delays to cybersecurity legislation and policy announcements have contributed to a perception that the issue is a low political priority, despite its growing importance to Britain’s economic and national security. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, an update to the country's critical-infrastructure cyber laws, took more than four years to reach Parliament and is now not expected to be enforced until 2028 — a decade on from the NIS Regulations it was written to replace. The core provisions of the CSRB had already been completed back in 2022 under Rishi Sunak, whose government incorrectly described the laws as “updated” before failing to include them in that year's King's Speech setting out the government’s parliamentary agenda and leaving the draft bill ultimately unintroduced to parliament. When Starmer's government first moved to bring the bill forward in September 2025, it was then delayed again amid a cabinet reshuffle. Separately, a set of ransomware proposals — mandatory reporting for all victims, a licensing regime for extortion payments and a ban on ransoms for critical infrastructure operators — was due to go out to consultation in mid-2024, before being scuppered when Sunak called a general election. Officials argue that the delays belie the substantial amount of work underway in Westminster. The government is expected to bring forward a new National Security Bill next year to reform the Computer Misuse Act — although some fear the reforms as proposed would fail to protect security researchers — as well as finally set the ransomware proposals on the statute books. In last month’s budget, the government committed £120 million ($159 million) over four years to the AI Security Institute and a further £40 million ($53 million) to establish a National Agentic Security Unit to address the threats posed by AI agents acting autonomously. Another £70 million ($93 million) was earmarked for an AI-powered vulnerability hunting center at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), with £60 million ($79 million) allocated to the first phase of Cyber Shield, a national defense system that would use AI agents to find and fix security weaknesses across government and critical infrastructure networks. Potentially more consequential for the technology industry was a commitment, buried among the budget announcements, that the government would consult next year on “where liability for cyber breaches should sit.” Ministers have also launched a voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge, seeking commitments from British businesses to put cybersecurity on the boardroom agenda and better manage their supply-chain risks. The government describes the pledge as a central pillar of the National Cyber Action Plan. National Cyber Action Plan The plan’s contents have not been officially disclosed. Recorded Future News understands it will include three pillars focusing on Threat, Growth and Resilience. The clearest public indication of the government’s approach came in a lecture to the Royal United Services Institute in June by the NCSC’s chief executive Richard Horne. Horne called for a full court press across what he termed the “near, mid and far spaces” of cyberspace — a framing people familiar with the plan expect to shape the areas it focuses on. He defined the near space as the defense of individual organizations, the far space as offensive action against adversaries and the “mid space” as the shared “cloud, technology and telecommunications infrastructure,” most of which he said was “in private hands.” In that space, he said, the government would partner with providers to “harden the mid space and disrupt attacker activity.” The idea of an action plan is to specifically set out how and when specific activities will be undertaken, rather than simply describing the overall strategy. Sources who spoke to Recorded Future News says the critical details would be in the plan’s implementation schedule. No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

13poxex.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 25, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr. The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below - CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request. CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules. Advisories for both the flaws were published on November 24, 2026, in the following versions - CVE-2026-120705: org.geoserver:gs-wfs-core - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 CVE-2026-120705: org.geotools:gt-metadata - 35.2, 34.6, and 33.7 CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 "Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today. Eye Security, which discovered and reported CVE-2026-120705, said the flaw can be combined with two other vulnerabilities in the same product to create an unauthenticated remote code execution chain - CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use of a hard-coded signing key ("geoserver") vulnerability in the "remember me" functionality that could be exploited to forge administrator authentication. (Fixed in org.geoserver:gs-main versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7) CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. (Fixed in org.geoserver.security:gs-sec-jdbc versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7) In a hypothetical attack chain, a bad actor can follow the steps below - Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml"). Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password. Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer. According to the project maintainers, CVE-2026-129245 is also part of a five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain that involves - CVE-2026-129244 (CVSS score: 6.9) - WFS stored query exception discloses data directory path CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - Service security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - Predictable "remember me" key allows administrator session forgery CVE-2026-129242 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Deserialization in JDBC user and role services allows administrator code execution "An attacker who obtains an administrator password digest, through any file disclosure or a copy of the data directory, can log in as that administrator," GeoServer maintainers said. "Changing the key in security/config.xml does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals the key." Jonah Burgess, a Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, who goes by the online alias CryptoCat has been acknowledged for independently discovering and reporting the five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain on August 2, 2026. "Prefixing the Web Feature Service (WFS) name, as in x/WFS, slips past the admin-only rule for stored queries. GeoServer turns escaped text in a saved query into live xi:include elements, which leaks the files holding the remember-me key and the admin password digest," the researcher said. "Those two values forge an administrator cookie without cracking the password. As admin, the attacker points a JDBC user service at an uploaded HSQLDB database, and the bundled driver deserialises a stored value that runs commands." In light of active exploitation of two of the flaws, users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, and 3.0.2 released over the past month as soon as possible. The development comes a little over three months after another critical flaw in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS score: 9.8) witnessed active exploitation efforts as a zero-day. (The story has been updated after publication to include more details of the flaws and emphasize that advisories for the issues were released on November 24, 2026. The patches were originally released in October and early November 2026.)

189wzuf.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 25, 2026Financial Security / Cybersecurity The U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has been hit by a cybersecurity incident that resulted in "unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," the bureau said on Tuesday. As a precaution, it has taken some systems offline. The bureau collects suspicious activity reports and other Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) filings from banks and other financial institutions and analyzes them to fight money laundering and terrorist financing. The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable. The agency has not named the systems it reached or those it took offline. To support filers affected by the disruption, the bureau is extending some filing deadlines: covered reports originally due between November 18 and December 29 can now be submitted until December 30. A relief order issued the same day, FIN-2026-R002, applies to three groups: Financial institutions that used Secure Direct Transfer Mode (SDTM), the channel for sending batches of BSA reports directly from their own servers, as of November 18 Companies required to file a beneficial ownership information report during the covered window Individuals required to update a FinCEN Identifier during the same window All other Bank Secrecy Act obligations stay in force, including the duty to monitor for suspicious transactions. The service alert says urgent suspicious activity information can still reach law enforcement through the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not affected by the disruption. The disclosure followed days of filing trouble. Filing providers reported failures in automated batch submissions beginning November 18, and the bureau posted a notice about the disruption to SDTM late last week, according to a filing outages report by the markets news site The Deep Dive. The bureau has not said whether the intrusion caused those outages. The order grants the relief because of a "service disruption" and does not mention the cybersecurity incident. Nor has the agency said when the access began, whether any data was viewed or taken, or who was responsible. No group has publicly claimed the intrusion so far. Those answers matter because of what the bureau holds: reports of suspicious financial activity filed by financial institutions nationwide. The incident is not Treasury's first in recent years: in December 2024, a China-linked group used a compromised BeyondTrust API key in an earlier Treasury breach that reached department systems and documents. No link between the two incidents has been reported.

12qr7uq.text: TL;DR More than 64% still valid after four years: GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that most valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, because teams stall on what a revoke will break. Validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets: Prioritize by impact instead, weighing what a credential can access and whether it leaked publicly, and update the risk score as new context arrives. Revoke last, never first: Issue a replacement, store it in the vault, switch every consumer to the vault call, deploy and monitor, then revoke the original and confirm it no longer authenticates. Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI connect securely to data, services, and each other. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, but credential remediation is where many secret security programs bog down. This is the second of three articles we are releasing to explain how we help address detection, remediation, and prevention. The first article in this series, “The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It,” covered detection across every surface where credentials live. Just knowing they exist is not enough. Teams need to take action to remediate those findings. To do that, they need context around every credential they find. Without the right context, it is impossible to know what risks the secret carries. It is also difficult to understand which systems rely on those secrets and the risk levels that revoking the secret brings. Nobody wants to break production, but we also cannot allow attackers to leverage those secrets. The resulting decision paralysis leaves many teams struggling to rotate immediately. Sometimes it can take years for the secret to be revoked finally. That is actually all too common, as shown by GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research that found that 64% of valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, a full 4 years later. It would be great if there were a one-size-fits-all solution for remediating every leak; in reality, each one is tied to a specific integration. What we can do is streamline the processes needed to get to the end, making it much easier for organizations of any size. And it does take the whole organization to properly deal with leaked secrets.
