Why credential remediation is so hard for so many teams A team that discovers an exposed credential rarely has all the authority or knowledge needed to fix it without causing further issues. A security engineer can see it’s valid and dangerous, but that security engineer usually cannot immediately tell which services will fail when it is revoked. Breaking production is considered a much higher risk than the possibility of a stolen and abused secret, so they need to go looking for answers, which is a time-consuming process. The developers who know where and why a key is used and, hopefully, how to rotate it safely are often busy shipping new features and managing existing requests from the business. An alert in their email that shows only a file path and a secret type asks those busy devs to stop their workflow and launch their own investigation. These requests, all too often, sink into the backlog. At the same time, the larger the organization, the harder it is to find the right person who knows the answer to “what breaks if this key is revoked?” Application security teams monitor code where keys are used, identity and access management (IAM) teams govern identities that were issued keys, and the Platform Engineering team runs the vaults holding the keys. They all have different perspectives and, in most organizations that are early in their secrets security maturity journey, can only tell part of the story. Endpoint security teams are also watching what happens at the workstation level. They are beginning to track secrets stored there, as software supply chain attacks have increasingly targeted these plaintext credential stores over the last couple of years. A secret leaked here might even be the triggering event for the rotation in case of compromise from an infostealer. The endpoint team is historically not connected to AppSec or Platform teams. One credential can touch all these teams while each individual, isolated group sees only its own slice of the credential layer. Now, multiply the communication and coordination issue across hundreds or thousands of potential leaks, and the scale of the remediation problem becomes clearer. Action before investigation invites downtime The risk of revoking before fully understanding the fallout is fairly high for the business. This is weighed against potential future abuse. Of course, this math changes during an active breach when the clock is ticking and when exfiltration or lateral movement is already occurring. Those emergencies do not get backlogged. Mature organizations understand that addressing leaks before an emergency arises is the better plan overall, but remediation times are still measured in weeks for most teams. How long a remediation process takes really boils down to how fast and accurately responders can gather and communicate information about the issue. Responders need to know a lot of things, starting with whether the credential works, what it can access, and who owns it before they can even ask questions like “where else does it appear?” and “which systems depend on it?” For example, envision two valid cloud credentials. One grants read-only access to a single storage bucket, and the second one is a root-level key with administrative control over production. While their privileges and dependent workloads determine the appropriate level of urgency, both require the same level of insight and investigation to triage the remediation process and decide whether the response is a rotation next sprint or a revocation this very second. The ultimate goal is to remove the leaked key rapidly, but in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds. Rotating secrets safely simply requires resources and a coordination plan. If this process is always piecemeal and manual, then mistakes are more likely to happen. A security team that causes an outage once will face resistance the next time it asks to rotate anything. Prioritize by impact, not just validity Validity is the first and clearest signal most responders look at. Alone, this is an incomplete signal. GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those secrets cannot be verified automatically. While validity still matters, access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency. If the leak happened publicly on the internet, that raises the urgency even further. Any risk scoring needs to explain which factors drove it. It also needs to be a living risk score, adjusting for new information as new context arrives. Scoring it once upon discovery is akin to trusting an initial CVSS score in a CVE disclosure. It is a helpful guide but needs to be updated based on what is really going on in your organization. The organization and its risk tolerance will decide what happens next. Having as much information centrally available as possible is key to a rapid response, as responders reach the boundaries of what systems they can actually touch. Route the work to the right people who can push the change Remediation requests should let the developer or platform team act immediately, without requiring the team to repeat the investigation that has already taken place. Any request to replace a key for a production system should include validity and known exposure locations. It should list dependencies too, and where possible show how it connects to business operations. The more the person picking up the request understands about the issue, the sooner they can act. In an ideal world, all remediation requests would be routed to their named owners. In the messy reality of the enterprise, you will likely need to involve the developer who leaked the secret and gather data from commit attribution or source metadata. We need to establish communication because there is a probability that they will need further instructions or guidance. Requests should not be ‘thrown over the fence’ and then forgotten about. Follow-up and confirmation about remediation progress should be centrally collected and shared so every department knows where the rotation process is at any given moment. This accountability proves resilience efforts when an auditor shows up. Engineers need to be enabled with a clean way to communicate once they start the work and once their ticket is ready to close. Routing the work through existing ticketing tools keeps it alongside other engineering work, but those tickets also need to integrate with the responder’s security operational tooling. Rotate, revoke, and vault: the order matters Safe rotation means following a specific set of steps, in the right order, so you don’t break anything. Remember: “Availability” is one of the legs of the CIA (confidentiality, integrity, availability) security triad. For mature organizations, this could be as straightforward as rotating the secret in a vault, since the production applications and systems relying on the credential are all already consuming it from the secrets manager. Any plaintext copies are then rendered harmless once the original offending secret is revoked. For organizations and situations where no existing vaulted copy is in use, this process often starts with issuing a replacement credential. If the responder can do this, they should do so immediately and store it safely in the vault. Then, replace every occurrence of the plaintext secret with that vault call, across every known consumer. The remediation steps from there are to push the changed code or config live and monitor for any issues, ready to roll back if anything breaks. Only when all the new systems are safely consuming the new vaulted credential appropriately can the team revoke the original. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident. GitGuardian’s service account credential rotation checklist covers these steps in detail. Verify the fix and keep the evidence Only close the ticket when the key is safely revoked, and the danger is removed. There needs to be an audit trail about what you fixed and how you proved that. You need verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Optionally, and depending on the circumstances, you can show that the old secret was removed from all surfaces. Any incidents closed while the credential remains valid deserve their own review queue. This common case happens when a team rotates a key in one system while the old key remains active and valid in another. This means a siloed team only accounted for their one occurrence in their tooling that lacks a unified view or relies on manual tracking. The incident record also serves auditors and security leaders. It shows what was found, who acted, and how long remediation took. One credential, start to finish with GitGuardian At GitGuardian, we have helped thousands of developers and organizations streamline their remediation process. To help visualize how we can help, imagine a Kubernetes application that calls an external service with an API key stored in a secrets manager. During troubleshooting in our imagined scenario, a developer copies the key into a local configuration file and commits it. This is a fairly common scenario we have seen play out many times. GitGuardian scanning finds the secret as soon as it is committed. The platform generates a new open incident and alerts the assigned team. An automatic validity check confirms the key is still active, and the Secret Analyzer lists its permissions. A presence check confirms the secret is still in the codebase. All these checks can be rerun as remediation progresses. For customers with full platform integrations, the GitGuardian Exploration Map shows a production workload depending on it, and fingerprint matching ties the committed value to the vaulted copy. The security team can bring that context to the owning developer and operations team. Once a replacement key is issued, everyone can track the progress of the rotation and see when the PR that accounts for the deployment configuration is pulling from the vault. There is no guessing about whether revoking the original will affect anything critical. GitGuardian then rechecks validity and confirms the committed copy is gone. The incident might also expose a pattern worth investigating across other teams. Has this same codebase seen similar incidents? Has the same user caused the same issue before? Are vaulted credentials ending up in unmanaged files on developer laptops on a regular basis? These all point to a wider issue that needs to be addressed to prevent further incidents and an increased remediation backlog. From fixing to preventing Remediation reduces risk one credential at a time. It also shows where exposures keep coming from. The third and final article in this series covers prevention, starting on developer machines and in AI coding workflows. Teams that want to see this remediation workflow can take an interactive tour of the GitGuardian platform. Take a Guided Tour of GitGuardian FAQ What is credential remediation? Credential remediation is the work of removing the risk from a leaked or exposed credential. The goal is to replace and revoke the leaked key quickly, in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds, and then to confirm the old credential no longer authenticates. Why does credential remediation take so long? The team that finds an exposed credential rarely has the authority or the knowledge to fix it alone. A security engineer can see the credential is valid and dangerous, but usually cannot tell which services will fail when it is revoked. The developers, identity, platform, and endpoint teams each see only their own slice of the credential layer, so responders spend their time gathering context instead of fixing the leak. How do you prioritize which leaked credentials to fix first? Prioritize by impact, not validity alone. GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that validation-only prioritization misses 46% of critical secrets, because some secrets cannot be verified automatically. Access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency, and a public leak raises it further. The risk score should explain which factors drove it and change as new context arrives. What is the safe order for rotating a leaked secret? Issue a replacement credential and store it in the vault. Replace every plaintext copy of the old secret with a call to the vault, across every known consumer. Push the changed code or configuration live and monitor for issues, ready to roll back. Revoke the original only when every system is consuming the new vaulted credential. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident. How do you verify that a leaked credential has been remediated? Close the ticket only when you have verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Keep an audit trail of what was fixed and how it was proved, including who acted and how long remediation took. Incidents closed while the credential is still valid deserve their own review, since a team may have rotated the key in one system while it stayed active in another.

98p9ic.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 25, 2026Web Security / Vulnerability The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by November 27, 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of remote code execution (RCE) impacting Drupal core. "Drupal Core contains a not failing securely vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to take over an existing site or execute arbitrary code via the Drupal installer," CISA said. "Under specific conditions, the attacker can use install.php to attempt to reinstall Drupal on the site." As previously reported by The Hacker News, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, resulting in site takeover or remote code execution under certain circumstances. According to an independent analysis by Searchlight Cyber, it has emerged that ordinary server resource limits can be abused to trick Drupal into mistakenly believing that an existing website was not installed, enter its installation process via "install.php," create an administrator-controlled account, and execute arbitrary PHP code. While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources. As a result, a failed database connection to the configured database and a failed database check for an existing installation are interpreted as evidence that the website has not been installed, and Drupal allows the installation to proceed after winning a race condition that allows a second database connectivity check to pass. To achieve this, the three resource exhaustion techniques have been put to use - EMFILE, which refers to a limit on how many files a Linux process can open Database connection exhaustion TCP source-port exhaustion "We started with EMFILE, then explored database and TCP limits to determine whether availability failures could become security primitives," the cybersecurity company said. "Applying this methodology to Drupal uncovered a pre-authentication RCE affecting Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 across four common deployment combinations: Apache with PostgreSQL, Apache with MySQL, PHP-FPM with PostgreSQL, and PHP-FPM with MySQL." This behavior can be turned into a pathway for code execution by taking advantage of the fact that Drupal's installer supports SQLite database files and allows the database path to be selected during installation. This is made possible because the installer doesn't restrict the file name extension. "By selecting a path ending in .php under the document root, the installer creates an SQLite database with a PHP extension," Searchlight Cyber said. "Once the installation reaches the site configuration form, Drupal stores the submitted website name inside the SQLite database. By using PHP code as the website name, the payload bytes are written into the .php database file." While direct access to the generated PHP file is blocked by Drupal's stock .htaccess on a stock Apache deployment, a path-handling weakness in the Apache RewriteRule could be exploited to achieve arbitrary PHP execution. "Starting from three system-wide limits, we showed how errors that appear to affect only availability can become primitives for crossing a security boundary," Searchlight Cyber researchers Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues said. "In Drupal, temporary database failures can produce a FAIL, FAIL, and then SUCCESS sequence that reopens the installer on an existing website and ultimately leads to pre-authentication RCE through an SQLite database containing PHP code." The issue has been addressed in the following versions - Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.13 Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.22 Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.22 The addition of CVE-2026-132165 to the KEV catalog follows a report received by the Drupal Security Team that it "was exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC." It's worth noting that CVE-2026-132165 is the third Drupal flaw to come under active exploitation this year following CVE-2026-9082 (CVSS score: 6.5) and CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: 6.5).

1mxqjjj.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 25, 2026Insider Threat / Artificial Intelligence A former OpenAI employee accused of concealing a covert recording device at the company's San Francisco offices will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, for allegedly bugging the artificial intelligence (AI) company's offices with the aim of recording sensitive conversations. Subsequent court filings have pointed out that Alfozan was in touch on WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi royal family, as well as expressed interest in moving back to Saudi Arabia following OpenAI's initial public offering (IPO). He has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the ChatGPT-maker said at the time. Alfozan pleaded not guilty to the charges during his appearance in San Francisco federal court earlier this month. According to CNBC, the decision comes after prosecutors told the court last week that they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia." However, they said investigators have found hundreds of audio files on the defendant's personal devices, including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that took place at OpenAI throughout September 2026. Some of these involved meetings with OpenAI customers and contained material protected by attorney-client privilege, prosecutors said, adding he possessed a photograph of what's believed to be a term sheet for a "strategic partnership" between OpenAI and another company. "What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation," they said. Under the bail conditions, Alfozan will be required to wear a GPS ankle monitor, observe a curfew from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., stay within the Northern District of California, and avoid airports and train and bus stations. He is expected to be released on Wednesday morning. "There is no spy story that we're talking about right now," U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse said, per The Wall Street Journal. "The government doesn't have that."

1a8chkx.text: An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm, the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from. The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request. Checks since then found no sign that any package was changed. Whether the attacker read account data such as email addresses, password hashes, and two-factor authentication secrets could not be ruled out, the team said. What Hex Users Should Do Now Everyone with a hex.pm account has been logged out because the maintainers replaced the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. They advise account holders to take these steps: Change your hex.pm password. Reset two-factor authentication by setting up a new authenticator entry, and store the new recovery codes. Log back in to the client with mix hex.user auth or, for Erlang projects, rebar3 hex user auth. Update the Hex client when the next release ships, expected within days, with a new registry signing system. Watch for phishing. Exposed email addresses may be misused, so check that links in any email about Hex go to hex.pm. API keys do not need to be replaced, according to the team: they are random 128-bit values stored only as HMAC-SHA256 hashes, which it says cannot realistically be brute-forced. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not stop it for weak passwords, so changing them still matters. Developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset, Peter Ullrich, one of the report's authors, said in a maintainer clarification on the Elixir Forum. Those who signed up with GitHub should still log back in to their clients, and reset two-factor authentication if they enabled it. Until the new client ships, the advice is to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and to avoid third-party mirrors. The registry signing key has not yet been replaced, and it was among the credentials the attacker could have read. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514 with the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, sat in the parser hex.pm used to read request bodies sent in an Erlang data format. That parser ran before routing and authentication, so an unauthenticated POST request to any address on the site could reach it. The decoding function was meant to be safe, and it did block dangerous terms such as functions, but it accepted maps with a __struct__ key, which allowed a request body to pose as any Elixir struct the application had loaded. The safety check that would have stopped this was removed from the code on February 23, 2016, which is where the flaw's age comes from. Exploitation before Monday has not been established. A crafted struct ran nothing by itself. It caused an error, and the error reporting code then inspected the struct. That inspection, via the Ecto and DBConnection database libraries, led to a point where the server called a function of the attacker's choice, which then ran operating system commands with the permissions of the registry's service account. The security advisory lists hex.pm as affected from February 23, 2016 until Monday. The fix commit makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, and every hex.pm server was running it by 18:31 UTC on Monday. Load balancer logs recorded 69 exploit requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC on Monday, all from two addresses, the Hex.pm team said in its incident report yesterday. Files created by the exploit appeared on six web servers, in one case just 3 milliseconds after the request. Three of those servers joined mid-attack, when a restart brought up machines still on the vulnerable build. To check the packages, the team compared every database table against a copy taken two minutes before the first exploit request and traced each difference to normal activity. The 23 releases published during the attack all match the audit log, no older release was changed, and the package and registry files written that evening match the database records. Database reads, shell commands, environment variables and direct reads from file storage were not logged. For that reason, "we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database," the team wrote. That database holds email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets and session data, and private packages could also have been read without leaving a trace. The checks found no leftover shells and no new accounts or cloud keys in the audit logs. Who was behind the attack is unknown. Activity from the two addresses going back to late last week suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against, according to the team. A separate security report describing the same flaw arrived by email at 19:07 UTC on Monday, after the attack had ended. By yesterday morning the team had replaced every credential the attacker could have read except the registry signing key. On Monday night it reported the breach to the Swedish data protection authority, to CISA in the United States and to ENISA in the European Union. Related Library Fixes Alongside the incident, maintainers of three widely used Elixir libraries disclosed flaws of their own involving structs built from untrusted data, and shipped fixed versions yesterday. These are separate disclosures, not further attacks on Hex.pm. Library CVE Affected versions Fixed versions ash CVE-2026-124283 3.31.3 up to, but not including, 3.38.0 3.38.0 db_connection CVE-2026-133555 1.1.0 up to, but not including, 2.10.3 2.10.3 flop CVE-2026-130411 From 0.8.0, each branch before its fixed version 0.26.7, 0.27.3, 0.28.1, 0.29.2 Each needs its own conditions to be exploited. The Ash flaw requires keyset pagination with a client-supplied cursor, certain sort field types, and a signing secret left at its unset default, according to the Ash advisory. The db_connection flaw "is not exploitable in db_connection alone," the DBConnection advisory says, because another component must first decode untrusted data into structs. The Flop flaw has similar conditions around its pagination cursors, according to the Flop advisory. The exploited flaw sits in the hexpm server code, not in the Hex client, so organizations that run their own copy of the registry are affected until they deploy the patch.

ozwnc6.text: An unknown threat actor has been using artificial intelligence (AI)-driven offensive tooling in a campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, impacting 22 distinct organizations across the world. The intrusion activity, tracked by GreyNoise under the moniker GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), is assessed to have targeted organizations in the financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing sectors across the U.K., Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the U.S. Confirmed attack activity has been recorded between October 17 and November 2, 2026, with the threat actor using 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control. Most of these IP addresses are associated with disposable network infrastructure. The campaign has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. It's suspected that the attackers are relying on agentic harnesses and systems for vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and automatic interaction with compromised assets. The threat actor has also been observed using tools like Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python scripts to carry out internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement on victim environments. "We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created," GreyNoise said. In one case, the attackers have been found using an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500, a critical flaw in Rejetto HFS, in early October 2026 to obtain control of the server and issue commands, including adding an SSH key to the "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys" file. Subsequently, GT13 is said to have used the compromised server as a relay for follow-on operations centered around saving command results and exfiltrating data from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. The attackers also unsuccessfully attempted to deploy a Linux implant named ZULT to the compromised Rejetto HFS server. "The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server," the cybersecurity company said. "We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets." The attackers also moved to burrow deeper into one of the victim networks, using a script for a now-patched Check Point flaw (CVE-2026-16232) to launch over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers to - Steal firewall databases and internal certificate authority files Mint a new certificate Unload security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections Conduct internal network reconnaissance and attempt lateral movement The post-compromise activity also involved attempts to target other enterprise systems, such as Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966), Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2024-21893), VMware vCenter (CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048), Microsoft Exchange (CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473), and Microsoft Netlogon (CVE-2020-1472). In tandem, the threat actor has attempted to exploit various other security flaws, including, but not limited to - CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure) CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler) CVE-2026-41089 (Windows Netlogon) CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF) GreyNoise has theorized that GT13 has in its possession a "mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus" that it uses to weaponize vulnerabilities, scan for susceptible assets, and exploit them to gain access to systems that can be later used as operational relays or true targets. "The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique," Sergey Shykevich, Director, Threat Intelligence at Check Point Software Technologies, told The Hacker News. "Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity."

15qy3s3.text: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August 2026 that have led to data theft and extortion attempts. The attacks have targeted financial services, healthcare, and legal services located in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia. Other targets include construction, high-technology, transportation, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, insurance, and real estate sectors. "The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal, or market consequences," Unit 42 said. "These attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September." The activity has been attributed to a number of threat clusters, including - Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters) CL-CRI-1116 (aka Redact, formerly BlackFile), first observed in January 2026 CL-CRI-1147 (aka Pink), first observed in May 2026 CL-CRI-1182 (aka Falcon), first observed in mid-2026 CL-CRI-1192 (aka Helix and UNC6671), first observed in June 2026 CL-CRI-1264 (aka Vortex), first observed in September 2026 CL-CRI-1274 (aka Cinder), first observed in September 2026 Intrusions typically commence with voice phishing, with the attackers posing as IT staff to resolve a purported authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page personalized to their organization. Once the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, abuse cloud utilities and, in a few instances, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims. The harvested authentication data is used to authenticate to victim environments, typically by routing such requests through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. They then seek to establish multi-layered persistence by registering their MFA devices, generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials, authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications; enumerate sensitive data; evade defenses by modifying mailbox rules and clearing security alert events; and harvest data from cloud platforms. "Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization," Unit 42 said. "These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices." CL-CRI-1264 has also been observed enrolling unauthorized MFA devices within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence, often reusing a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. The attack chains involve automated data exfiltration using Python scripts to harvest information from Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint. Once data is exfiltrated, the threat actor sends Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and instructing them to visit a TOR-hosted ransom negotiation site. The second new cluster to emerge around the same time is CL-CRI-1274, which has also leaned on vishing for initial access and leveraged the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim's SharePoint and OneDrive environments. "Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site," Unit 42 said. The cybersecurity company said it also observed the CL-CRI-1192 attackers using a malicious browser extension named "Google Chrome" that's said to have been sideloaded onto the browser after enabling Developer Mode. The add-on performs a number of malicious actions, such as - Installing global keyloggers Stealing local/session storage and authentication cookies for Microsoft and Google accounts Scanning pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens Streaming webcam feeds Implementing a command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol to capture screenshots, dispatch input events, steal clipboard contents, and allow remote site navigation. "We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge," Unit 42 said. "The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this." One of the defining traits of the threat actors is their use of "apex" domains that impersonate single sign-on (SSO) portals, IT support pages, and passkey configuration services for each of the targeted organizations. Also shared among the attackers is an AitM phishing kit called Doko's Panel that allows them to steal authenticated sessions and then abuse them to access connected software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms like SharePoint, Salesforce, DocuSign, and Slack to exfiltrate data of interest. "The same persona behind Doko's Panel has been observed actively recruiting 'experienced callers' via Telegram, specifying requirements including fluent English with no accent, and advertising six-to-seven-figure weekly returns — evidence of the professionalized vishing-as-a-service model that complements the phishing kit ecosystem," Push Security noted in a report published earlier this May. Microsoft has also revealed cloud-based intrusions in which threat actors have employed passkey and SSO lures to obtain unauthorized access and add their own authentication methods to set up persistence, as well as conduct high-volume Microsoft Graph activity, SharePoint and OneDrive downloads, and mailbox collection through REST APIs. "Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments," Unit 42 said. "Cybercriminals like Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors are pivoting away from encryption, enabling them to move at greater speed across their intrusion lifecycle while still achieving their objectives."

5f9smh.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 25, 2026Web Security / Malware WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account. The WordPress plugins team has independently detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent." The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below - Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress (2.9.1 – 2.9.4) WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress (1.7.4) Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms (2.6.3) Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable (2.5.4) Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion (1.6.4) Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce (1.0.2) These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched. "Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said. Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval(). It can also perform the following actions - Accept queued commands that run shell commands Read, write, and delete arbitrary files Query arbitrary database tables Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal. Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible. "Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally." The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors. The site carried "thirteen separate ClickFix injections from three distinct kits [LOM, ErrTraffic, and Macfinger], alongside seven further malicious loaders," it said. "Several of the injections attempt to remove each other's code and overlays, and one injection disables another through a JavaScript naming collision. Five of the thirteen injections resolve their next-stage infrastructure from Polygon smart contracts, a technique known as EtherHiding."

ngwx2k.text: A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus. Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025. Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to harvest email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations. The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). "While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments." This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives. Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel. This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. "This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said. As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia. A Windows backdoor, KuboShell, uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network. "On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained. "KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token." Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server. It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds. Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process - PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown. "We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said. The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe." "Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention." "If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

191ekr.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 24, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication. The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir"). "A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today. The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam, XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw. Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5). The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5). The issues have been addressed in the following versions - VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2 VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300 VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract) VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - Fixed in 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) The fixes arrive days after Broadcom shipped updates for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), another authentication bypass flaw impacting the VMware Directory Service that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group called Armory Castle. VMware has noted that CVE-2026-123903 is a distinct issue and is not related to CVE-2026-123890. While Broadcom makes no mention of any of the newly disclosed flaws as being exploited in the wild, it's essential that customers apply the updates for optimal protection.

1h4o26o.text: A threat cluster previously assessed to be affiliated with the ShinyHunters extortion crew may have rebranded and continued operations under a new name called INCEPTION, according to Okta's Threat Intelligence team. The cluster, dubbed O-UNC-053, is characterized by the use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Okta said it's been tracking the group since March 2026. The identity and access management provider said targets of this cluster previously had stolen data published to the ShinyHunters data leak site (DLS). However, as of November 16, 2026, a new data leak site operating under the name INCEPTION has listed the data siphoned from O-UNC-053 targets. "While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion," Okta researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said in a report shared with The Hacker News. Social engineering and credential harvesting attacks mounted by O-UNC-053 have targeted a broad range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, biotechnology, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality, and legal. Similar to O-UNC-066 and UNC6671, the newly identified cluster also relies on a phishing kit to intercept authentication flows and capture a user's credentials and MFA codes. However, the kit is not designed to bypass phishing-resistant methods like passkeys and Okta FastPass. "While interacting with targeted users on the phone, the operators socially engineer them into sharing factors like one-time passcodes and approving push notifications," Okta said. "If successful, the operators gain access to SaaS applications and exfiltrate sensitive data, which is often used to extort targets under the threat of releasing it on a data leak site." Domains created by the group are registered through NiceNIC, Spaceship, Tucows, and NameSilo, with the domain names using the following patterns - legal-<target>[.]com legaldept-<target>[.]com <target>[.]legal <target>-legal[.]com The use of "legal" themes in these attacks is said to have started in October 2026, and is often registered on or within a day of a campaign starting. Prior campaign waves have employed help desk-, support-, and claims-related themes for the registered domains. These findings also dovetail with an alert from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which has warned of widespread vishing activity using legal-themed domains that either begin with "legal-" or end with "-legal" using the ".com" top-level domain. More than 70 such domains have been observed since October 2026, it said, adding each domain is specifically created for an intended target operating in different industries, like cryptocurrency, financial services, healthcare, high technology, and hospitality, among others. "Registered in rapid evening batches and shielded behind Cloudflare, these web-only domains deploy a filtered kit that delivers tailored content to intended victims while routing visitors it is not configured to attack to the targeted organization's legitimate Okta or NetIQ sign-in flow," ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons said. Some of the confirmed domains linked to the activity are listed below - legal-pepsico[.]com legal-paychex[.]com legal-duolingo[.]com activisionblizzard-legal[.]com legal-westernunion[.]com legal-dropbox[.]com legal-indeed[.]com legal-creditkarma[.]com legal-amd[.]com legal-grubhub[.]com legal-twitch[.]tv The crux of the campaign is to tailor the landing page to the specific identity provider of the target, while filtering unwanted visitors and forwarding them to the organization's authentication infrastructure, such as Okta. "Throughout our tracking of O-UNC-053 between March and September 2026, we observed the names of targeted entities appear on the ShinyHunters DLS between 1 and 28 days after the phishing infrastructure was registered," Okta noted. However, it's unclear at this stage if the published data on the INCEPTION site is authentic and whether they are running the site themselves or are collaborating with another extortion gang. The exact nature of the relationship between ShinyHunters and O-UNC-053 is also unknown. It's worth noting that the ShinyHunters data leak site went offline in late September 2026 following the arrest of three alleged members of the group, including a Canadian co-conspirator responsible for the breach of the FBIjobs.gov portal. There is no evidence of data from O-UNC-053 targets being published on any data leak site from early September 2026 through October and early November 2026, until listings for multiple targets appeared on the INCEPTION site last week. "This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors," Okta said. "Regardless of the nature of the relationship with the INCEPTION DLS, O-UNC-053 remains active in conducting vishing attacks against targets in an effort to take over accounts, steal data, and extort targets."

1wvbpq4.text: The Hacker NewsNov 24, 2026Supply Chain Security / DevSecOps Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it. In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check. The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it. The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it. That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't. Immutability Is Not Provenance Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected. GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it. But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered: Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned. Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project. Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen. With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely. GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job. GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later. That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server. Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you. What You'll Learn Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers: What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions Who Should Attend Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you. Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either. Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

16c1pii.text: A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday. The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398. Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared. VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework. The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face. The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects. To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis. Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox." The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host. The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image. The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it. "This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced. The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet. Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks. The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights. The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE. What to patch On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it. .NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694. Flaw Affected Fixed in CVE-2026-87268 (VirtualBox) VirtualBox 7.2.16, Windows hosts Oracle's September update, build 7.2.18 CVE-2026-108398 (.NET Framework) .NET Framework 4 on Windows, UMCI case tested on Windows 11 S Mode October 13 update, per-version KB Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.
