9uomss.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 24, 2026Cloud Security / Vulnerability Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. "An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been." The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses. According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected. "On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory. "Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include - Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers Subscription keys Tokens used to call direct management APIs As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

1omkg7k.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 24, 2026Web Security / Vulnerability A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed. The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three. Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet. The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline. The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time. Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release. Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation. The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says. The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says. It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails. All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon. For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to: Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu. Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache. Update to a fixed release. The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough. This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

vu2wqr.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 24, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Vulnerability OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime. "It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X. The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption. The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software. Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service. The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation. To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it. "eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said. "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)." Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations. Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded. "Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands." This involves the following steps - An agent is tasked with finding new vulnerabilities in an application, or working off external sources of new vulnerability disclosures. Shirudo on the operator machine builds a security shield consisting of eBPF or application bytecode after reproducing and validating the exploit. The shield is delivered as signed .bee packages via an OCI-compliant registry. The Shirudo layer on each target pulls these .bee packages, validating each signature using TPMs to establish trust and safety. In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said. OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed. "We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before." "Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative."

1r1stu6.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The critical vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services. CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution. The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026. As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored. "N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity." CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China. "In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step." Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server. "In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root." Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network. The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, and AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge, revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft - AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization. AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain. AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access. In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework. "The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said. "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection." According to Datadog Security Labs, ARTEX also appears under other names like ScopeWeaver, LUCK — 自主资产控制台 (LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console), and 观澜SEC渗透测试平台 (Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform). In-the-wild activity involving ARTEX has also targeted several AWS environments with an aim to access financial data. Initial access vectors used in these attacks include compromised long-term AWS access keys and public Cognito user pools, with the latter being used to register an account, collect tokens, and enumerate AWS accounts. "In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents," security researcher Julie Agnes Sparks said. "The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like fund, invoice, billing, and LLC." Telemetry data gathered by Previdian from its sensors has recorded 52 HTTP requests containing explicit ARTEX markers between October 18 and November 15, 2026, from 10 source IP addresses. "Further investigation of these sources identified 3,651 related HTTP records involving application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal and attempts to retrieve sensitive configuration data," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said. "The most significant activity targeted Oracle WebLogic, Langflow, and Flowise, with additional payloads associated with Apache Struts, Log4j, and PHPUnit." Interestingly, one of the IP addresses associated with ARTEX activity, 31.22.91[.]156, overlaps with the AWS-documented campaign targeting AI infrastructure, including Langflow exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2025-3248. nc5a7u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks. The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence. First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations. One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure. The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026. "The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions." The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN." One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity. It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response. The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark. Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below - Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB. Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII. What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth. "It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools. "We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

henuhc.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Cybersecurity News / Hacking A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open. This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need. The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week. ⚡ Threat of the Week Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines. 🔔 Top News Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks. Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners." Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue. New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account. GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild. Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser). 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars 6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers. 8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts. Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them. 📰 Around the Cyber World Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers. A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India. The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs. Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries. Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism. Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed. Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027. Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days." Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both." Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025. Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences." At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service." Conclusion The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done. That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

11hm4t6.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Vulnerability / Open Source A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1. "Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD). "Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled." According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation. The parser options include - length lengthInBytes key tag offset, and the alias passed to namely() "Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead." CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters. "[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

1ssinmv.text: Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers. The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host. "On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said. The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine. The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames. In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload. What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder. It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation. The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed. Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online. "Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said. "As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026." Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. "An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs." "A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

eax96a.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 23, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for managed service providers. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw. It allowed a user with high-level API access to open connections to internal systems of the user's choosing on the platform's servers. The company fixed the flaw and restored access to the dashboard and APIs late on Saturday, closing an outage that began last Monday. Email delivery and spam filtering kept working throughout, according to the company. It has not said whether the flaw was the attackers' way in. The bug sat in a connection check that Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronization when a relay is configured. Before the fixed build, nothing restricted that check's destination, so the server could be pointed at any internal host and port to see which ones answered. "An authenticated API user can cause the server to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.," the vendor's security advisory says. The advisory gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3, and lists builds earlier than 20261121.1943 as affected, with that same build as the fix. It does not claim code execution. N-able informed customers of a service disruption last Monday and initially traced it to platform configuration and service dependencies, according to its incident timeline. Last Wednesday, the company said the outage was, in fact, a security incident: an unauthorized party had accessed one of the Hosted Cloud servers. The dashboard and APIs were kept offline as a precaution while it investigated. It responded by taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' existing API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and resetting local users' passwords. The company says it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including tenants' mailboxes, and no sign of exploitation beyond that one server since the fix was implemented. The investigation is still open, and the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident, according to the company. In that earlier incident, it took its hosted remote-monitoring platform offline on November 9 after a researcher published 33 unpatched flaws. For hosted customers, the work now is reconnecting. Scripts and integrations that used the revoked API tokens or OAuth tokens will need new credentials. The exact steps differ by setup: each partner has been emailed guidance specific to its environment, and anyone who has not received it is asked to contact support. The hosted platform itself is already patched, according to yesterday's incident update, so there is nothing for Hosted Cloud users to install. SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware, with software updates applied on a weekly schedule, according to the product's update documentation. The incident statements describe the Hosted Cloud only, so Local Cloud operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943. What the account so far does not say is how the attackers first got in, or whether any of the credentials they may have reached were actually taken. An outside digital forensics and incident response team has been brought in, and the company says a formal root cause analysis is due within two weeks of yesterday's update. Separate restoration times for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization, which were being brought back in phases, have not been given.

145kxup.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Cybersecurity researchers have urged users to discontinue using a legacy ASP.NET anti-CSRF library named Idunno.AntiCsrf ("Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll") following the discovery of a critical vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-131914, carries a CVSS score of 9.3 out of 10.0. The issue affects versions 0.9.1.0 and 0.9.1 Beta, and relates to an insecure deserialization vulnerability in the Idunno.AntiCsrf.AntiCsrfModule HTTP module. Idunno.AntiCsrf is a third-party ASP.NET IHttpModule designed to provide double-submit cookie Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection for ASP.NET WebForms applications. The open-source project is currently defunct and has not been updated since December 2008. At its core, the problem stems from the fact that the module deserializes untrusted CSRF form token data using an unkeyed .NET System.Web.UI.ObjectStateFormatter instance without cryptographic MAC or signature verification when handling incoming HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms (System.Web.UI.Page) endpoints. This behavior, in turn, can allow a remote attacker to achieve arbitrary remote code execution (RCE). Google's Mandiant division has given the vulnerability a "High" exploitability assessment, adding that exploitation hinges only on a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token. LDB, Genwei Jiang, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, Brian Bahtiarian, and Lucas Kossack of Google Cloud and Mandiant Incident Response have been credited with discovering the flaw earlier this month. "A remote attacker can supply any non-empty value in the configured CSRF cookie alongside a Base64-encoded .NET ObjectStateFormatter gadget chain in the configured CSRF form field to execute arbitrary code in the context of the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe), resulting in complete compromise of the web application server," Google-owned Mandiant said in an alert issued last week. "Active exploitation in the wild has been observed." Google's threat intelligence team did not disclose any further details related to the activity. The Hacker News has contacted Google, and we will update the story if we hear back. In the absence of an official patch, organizations still using the library are advised to discontinue its use and replace it with an actively supported anti-CSRF alternative such as follows - System.Web.Helpers.AntiForgery ASP.NET WebForms Page.ViewStateUserKey combined with MAC-verified/encrypted ViewState on postback forms ASP.NET Core Anti-Request Forgery (IAntiforgery) "Audit all ASP.NET Web.config files and bin/ directories for references to Idunno.AntiCsrf or AntiCsrfModule, and review IIS logs for anomalous POST requests to .aspx endpoints returning HTTP 302 or HTTP 500 with elevated cs-bytes (where logged)," Google said. "Environments with evidence of exploitation should rotate all secrets stored in Web.config and applicationHost.config (including <machineKey> keys, encryption keys, and database credentials) and inspect webroots for unauthorized files."

1pbhpss.text: Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud remote management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM devices, the maker of travel routers and remote-access KVM hardware said in a security notice updated today. The company identified and fixed the flaw on Friday and blocked the access the attacker used, so devices can no longer be infected through this route. The cloud-side fix does not remove malware from devices that were already infected, so owners still need to check their hardware and install the security firmware listed today. A KVM is a small device used to control a computer remotely as if sitting in front of it. The company is still investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were affected. It has not said how many devices were infected, when the attacks began, or how its cloud service was breached. It is emailing customers it identifies as affected, but owners do not need to wait for a message to act. A model missing from the firmware table below is not necessarily unaffected, the notice says, and owners should not install firmware meant for another model. RemoteToHome Consulting, a security consultancy that examined the incident on routers it manages, says in its incident investigation that it verified a root-level reverse shell on one of its GL-AXT1800 routers. The shell started on Friday evening and connected to 170.39.226[.]219, and two more owners reported the same shell on the same model and firmware, 4.8.3, with GoodCloud switched on. On GL-MT6000 routers, the same shell command ran but the connection never completed. On other routers the firm manages, a one-off command searched for files linked to a KVM implant and reported the result to the same address. The shell leaves no files behind, and its traces vanish when the device restarts, per the firm's reverse-shell analysis. The process marker the vendor published was absent on the router with the verified shell. After the researchers filed an abuse report late last week, the hosting provider told them it had suspended the server behind the address and preserved its data. The shell arrived through the GoodCloud client software on the router itself, according to the firm's technical analysis. A handler in that client takes two values from a cloud message and runs them as root through the shell without checking them. The vendor has not confirmed that finding. The unchecked code has been in the firmware since at least December 5, 2024, when it appeared in a GL-MT3000 release. It runs whether or not AstroWarp, the SD-WAN feature it belongs to, is in use, and its presence since 2024 does not mean attacks began then. The researchers reported a second, separate weakness in the cloud client to the vendor yesterday and are withholding details until it is fixed. One KVM owner described an infected GL-RM1 in an owner's report. Starting on Thursday, the device downloaded a script and two programs from 66.245.219[.]252, looked up the copycat domain gl-inet[.]top, and scanned the local network. It also kept connecting to 65.20.71[.]131, which the owner suspects was a command channel. The owner did not keep the downloaded files, and the method by which the device was infected has not been confirmed. The vendor advises checking the computer attached to an infected KVM for unfamiliar programs, accounts, startup items, and unusual network activity. The investigation also found an unrelated, older backdoor on 49 of the routers the firm manages, installed in batches between September 2025 and May 2026 by a route that is not known. Nothing so far links it to last week's attacks. How to Check a Device GL.iNet's check looks for one marker: a running process whose details contain the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log. A line showing only the grep command itself is not a match. Router, web panel: sign in to LuCI under System → Advanced Settings, open Status → Processes, and search for tmp/.log. Router, SSH: run ps | grep tmp. KVM: open the device's own terminal under Toolbox → Terminal → Access, then run ps -a | grep tmp on the RMQ1 or ps -aux | grep tmp on other models. Run it on the KVM, not on the attached computer. Check before rebooting or upgrading where compromise is suspected, the researchers advise, because the shell's traces disappear at restart. The marker can also miss infected devices: it was absent on the router with the verified shell. Before running netstat on a suspect device, check that /bin/netstat is still a link to busybox. The command itself may have been swapped, a forum warning and the researchers' indicator list say, and running a compromised copy starts the malware. The notice also points to an unofficial community check script, with the warning that the vendor has not reviewed it and that it can run with administrative privileges. Fuller indicators are in the researchers' detailed findings. What the Update Does and Does Not Remove GL.iNet listed stable security firmware for its router and KVM lines in the security notice it updated today, which now says the update "removes the malware identified in this incident without requiring a factory reset," with settings kept. That replaces earlier guidance, which offered a factory reset for infected devices ahead of the firmware's release. Model(s) Minimum fixed version GL-MG1300, GL-MT3000, GL-MT6000 4.11.1 GL-E5800 4.10.3 GL-BE3600, GL-BE9300 4.10.2 GL-BE14000 4.9.3 GL-BE6500, GL-MT3600BE, GL-MT5000 4.9.1 GL-BE10000 4.8.7 GL-AX1800, GL-AXT1800, GL-SFT1200, GL-X3000, GL-XE3000 4.8.4 GL-MT2500 / GL-MT2500A, GL-X2000 4.7.14 RM1, RM1V2, RM10, RM10RC, RM1PE, RM4PE (KVM) 1.10.3 RMQ1 (KVM) 1.8.7 In spot checks today, The Hacker News found the GL-MT3000 and GL-RM1 builds available at the vendor's router downloads and KVM downloads pages. The update is not shown to cover everything a root-level attacker may have left behind. In RemoteToHome's KVM firmware analysis, upgrading an RM1 to the earlier 1.10.2 security build with settings kept carried the device's password file, SSH keys and user directory across, and that directory holds scripts that run at every boot. Whether a planted script survives the upgrade has not been tested. For a device with signs of compromise, the researchers' advice is a firmware reinstall without keeping settings, and treating every stored secret as exposed: VPN keys, Wi-Fi and admin passwords, cloud credentials and SSH keys. The vendor's notice and that advice differ on this point. Until a device is updated, the option the researchers describe is switching GoodCloud off, after first securing another way to reach the device. Switching it off stops the cloud client from running but does not clean a device that was already infected. The attacker's identity, the number of affected devices, and how the cloud service itself was breached remain unknown, and The Hacker News found no CVE identifier for the flaw as of publication.

16slefe.text: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country. This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts. "In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week. The incidents have been found to include the following methods - Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs. Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes. Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert. Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records. CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor. The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions - Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths. Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information. Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel. Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems. Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks. "Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity." The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as the national nodal agency disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets. "In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools." Earlier this month, the agency also warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial ​firms and has used offensive penetration testing tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, and CyberStrikeAI to automate the intrusions at machine speed. According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the attacks have targeted banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintech companies, leading to multi-crore (equivalent to 10 million) unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs. "Perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers / IT systems to compromise the infrastructure," I4C said. "Hackers then target automated fund disbursement systems or special interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers. The money is sent to 'mule' accounts (accounts used by criminals) across different banks and then quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT." India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has also alerted of rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure, urging banks to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month. The Surge in AI Attacks The advisories also come at a time when organizations around the world are being targeted using AI tools, giving attackers a way to "execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity." Last week, the European Commission confirmed that attackers armed with ARTEX broke into its HR, medical reimbursement, and translation systems. The first signs of the attack were detected on October 22, 2026. ARTEX has also been implicated in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and Barracuda, with the latter revealing that a financially motivated criminal weaponized an exposed valid cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor to map its reach, repurpose discovered secrets to access more systems and look for seed phrases, and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets. "In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours [between November 1 and 2]. The work was methodical and tireless," Barracuda said. "The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match ARTEX." Frameworks like ARTEX manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute, and adapt tactics across multiple kill chain stages, including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. They can translate tactical goals described in natural language into machine commands that are executed by specialized AI agents. It integrates with various external LLMs, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, SpaceXAI Grok, Zhipu GLM, and Kimi. "ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an alert this month. "The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale." Check Point, in a report published this month, said it uncovered more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX, with attackers leveraging the tool to conduct opportunistic, financially-motivated cybercrime. "Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target," the company said. Data security firm Cohesity said threat actors using ARTEX are gaining access to systems that receive less security attention, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales support applications, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications built by individual business units. "In a research network we operate, a threat actor linked to Rhysida used an AI framework to rewrite tools in response to obstacles, often within minutes, and more than 150 versions of a single script reached a domain controller within a day," it said. In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits. The AI framework, called "exploit_agent," integrates with multiple frontier and local large language models (LLMs). It's designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention. The attacker, suspected to be Russian-speaking, is said to have leveraged the framework to target French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector. "The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software," Mandiant and GTIG said. "It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention." Some of the other notable incidents where AI agents and models do the legwork are listed below - Use of CAIRN in intrusion activity against targets, including in the aerospace sector in the U.S. Embedding LLMs into influence operation workflows to produce synthetic media, create convincing virtual personas, and generate and publish content. Use of Google's Gemini API, along with tools from multiple AI providers, to build an end-to-end influence-as-a-service (SaaS) platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, specifically across Europe and the Middle East. Use of LLMs by a China-linked contractor called Leaky Castle to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data Abuse of a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure by a China-nexus threat actor to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents. Use of LLMs by North Korean threat actors to generate resumes and prepare for job interviews at Western organizations. Creation of fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms by a suspected North Korean hacking group called Midnight Neptune (previously UNC1069) in attacks aimed at cryptocurrency entities in North America and Europe using job- and ClickFix-themed lures. These personas have been found to direct targets to fraudulent meeting platforms, which are used to run diagnostic fix scripts via ClickFix. "Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor," Google said. Use of CyberStrikeAI ("43.240.29[.]11") between September 30 and October 16, 2026, to validate stolen AWS credentials, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, and send a remote command. "The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded," Elastic Security Labs said. Use of Hermes, in combination with DeepSeek, by a threat actor called Silent Lynx in cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026 to assist with reconnaissance, data collection, and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems. Use of ARTEX to exploit a vulnerable custom PHP upload function and stage a web shell, and use it to access secrets and API keys, and ultimately compromise a company's development pipeline to alter a Git repository and deploy an attacker-controlled Kubernetes pod. Use of an AI coding assistant to revive a stalled attack at a U.S. retail organization and come up with ways to bypass defenses and steal credentials after their commands were blocked by security software in late September 2026. The attack is assessed to be financially motivated, based on the threat actor's scans for passwords in point-of-sale scripts and an IP address overlap with a prior campaign targeting online retailers. Use of CAIRN by a Chinese-speaking attacker between August and September 2026 and pairing it with GLM and DeepSeek models to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attacks, attributed to CL-STA-1238, have targeted advanced semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy, and civil society sectors, achieving unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the entities, including valid credentials, personal data, military and government identities, and the creation of persistent administrator accounts in a production system. "CAIRN coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Confirmed findings accumulate as immutable facts, and the agent queues its next actions as intents." Use of ARTEX to gain access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. "Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure," Cloudflare said. "LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments." Use of ARTEX to generate deepfake videos to trick identity verification checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges and steal AI credentials at "industrial scale" to gain free access to models. Amazon has characterized the second campaign as a "self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting." Targets include LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow (CVE-2025-3248), RAGFlow (CVE-2026-28797), Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. Use of CAIRN by a suspected Chinese-nexus threat actor to discover a zero-day vulnerability (GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94) in MONAI Label, a medical imaging application, and use it to gain complete control of a server within 11 minutes. The activity was detected in September 2026. "An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. The agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints." What's notable about accelerating AI-enabled attacks is that the technology is not just used as a force multiplier but has also emerged as the target. "The integration of AI-enabled tools into enterprise workflows is creating new attack surfaces, particularly where those tools hold privileged access to code, credentials, data, or connected applications," Recorded Future said. "Developer tools are a primary target of attacks on AI systems. Threat actors exploited weak access controls and software supply-chain vulnerabilities to steal data or establish persistence." Besides automating the time-consuming phases of intrusions, LLM-driven pentesting frameworks also lower the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks. "Now, an attacker can give an agent a goal in plain language," GitGuardian said. "The agent can investigate the environment, select tools, execute commands, interpret the results, and decide what to try next. The tools are also becoming better at recovering from failed attempts. An agent can encounter an error, interpret the response, modify its next command, and continue investigating." "Anyone with access to AntiFox or ARTEX can just verbally say into the dictation, 'find exposed credentials, determine what they access, and identify valuable resources.' That incantation initiates a series of technical actions that previously required considerably more hands-on expertise."

q63v93.text: Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week. Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored. OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said. The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said. The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it. The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack. The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls. One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server. On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections. "A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer. The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found. The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys. One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt. A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab. A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint. Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt. In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.
