The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties. The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week. Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted. What the Providers Have Disclosed An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections. Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated. A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window. At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts. Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers. Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three. The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week. What Users Should Do The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price. Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check. Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys. A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

1dwe0eu.text: A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it. Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly. Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks. Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses. The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files. The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering. Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor. WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index. Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory. WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other. Updating the Renderer The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced. Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system: Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix. Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell. One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point. The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

pivlb6.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Artificial Intelligence A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown. The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts. The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer. There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach. Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage." In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up. From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown. That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent. The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines. Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through. The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in. The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

1dc8sa6.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program. Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages. The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out. Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says. The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG. When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details. The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier. What to Update The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. What to install depends on where the library sits: Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory. Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible. Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch. Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases. GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed. The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

aqj2tu.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cyber Espionage Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week. The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled. The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install. MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework. The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder. The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected. Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history. Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report. The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company. Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it. A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root. That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do. In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise. The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot. Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install. The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw. What to Do Now With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach: Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs. Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default. Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to. Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched. If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used. The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described. The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

10d76gs.text: Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete." The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen. It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature. Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." "The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy." The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk. Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android). "However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said. "Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system." Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data. Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users - Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup. On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications. In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post. "We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said. "In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents." Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings. Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

19fccy5.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026) CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025) CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026) Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884. The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor. The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

1ghlyk1.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4. The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said. The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue. When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful. Also addressed by the company are two other flaws - CVE-2026-102769 - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted. CVE-2026-44908 - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70. Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message. It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. "Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation." WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

fb56hx.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale. Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan. "Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping." One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background. Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API. One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities - Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store. One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed - A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager A downloader that directly downloads the main payload It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them. "Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]." The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically. "Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging." "When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon." Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely. Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels - Control, which is used to issue commands Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft - call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones contacts, to collect contact information device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands file_manager, to access the file system input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy push, to create and manage local Android notifications screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards toast, to display text messages on the device's screen twofa, to capture one-time verification codes uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian. "ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application." "Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest." ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data. "What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said. Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers. Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure. An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features - Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device Abuse accessibility services for full remote control Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password "The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said. "To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off." Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations. "By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. 1aqcvsf.text: Every image scan returns hundreds of CVEs; the question is which ten your containers actually execute and which base image would zero the list entirely. We scored ten options with context and elimination weighted above raw detection. Evaluating scanners alongside the Top 10 Best Container Security Tools in 2026 reveals that static vulnerability counts alone do not prevent attackers who compromise container hosts through misconfigurations. Aqua’s Trivy takes 1 as the free floor everyone should run; Sysdig and Wiz complete a podium built on making findings mean something. Key Takeaways • 1 overall: Trivy the ubiquitous free scanner with platform depth above it. • Podium: Trivy (floor), Sysdig (in-use runtime filtering), Wiz (graph exposure ranking). • Strategy pick: Chainguard’s zero-CVE bases beat scanning by removing what scanners find. • One-vendor note: Grype and Syft are Anchore’s OSS pair SBOM-first scanning free. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based: detection quality, SBOM support, context/prioritization, registry/workflow fit, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. Project owners still need to reproduce suspected flaws and test suggested fixes before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. h8nhhs.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 28, 2026Password Management / Cyber Attack Cross-platform password manager pCloud Pass has confirmed it was targeted by a cyber attack after users reported seeing unknown devices being connected to their accounts. "A cyber attack targeting pCloud Pass occurred, which was promptly contained by the pCloud team," the Swiss company said in response to a number of posts on Reddit. "Unfortunately, a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and login attempts were made. Our system sends a notification automatically to each of these addresses." pCloud emphasized that user data was not compromised in the attack, adding passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass are encrypted and can only be accessed after providing a Master Password. It also said the incident was limited to pCloud Pass, and that pCloud Cloud Storage services are not affected. "With the advancement of AI, vulnerabilities in the software that every online service relies upon (such as operating systems, programming languages, and libraries) are being discovered faster than ever - sometimes even before the developers themselves identify them and release a fix," the pCloud Team said. pCloud has also urged users to stay alert for phishing attacks that may trick recipients into entering their Master Password or recovery words by email, phone, or chat. The development comes after numerous Reddit users reported receiving email alerts about a new device signing in to their pCloud Pass, despite having two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled, along with an option to "Open Settings" and change their Master Password if the action was not from them. In all observed cases, a device named "pd" has been found to connect from the following two IP addresses belonging to pCloud's own infrastructure in Luxembourg - 45.131.244[.]7 ("eapi1.pcloud.com") 45.131.247[.]10 ("onlyoffice.pcloud.com") However, it's unclear if the sign-in "attempts" were successful and if the attackers managed to access or download the encrypted vaults. pCloud also has not disclosed how the attackers got in, when the intrusion occurred, and for how long they had access before it was detected. One Reddit user by the name "antenore" has also reported that the "Open settings" button in the email message "goes through pass.pcloud.com/track, but the base64 redirect inside it decodes to https://passqa1.pcloud.com/?#/preferences. That looks like an internal QA environment, and it does not load (ERR_CONNECTION_ABORTED)." The Hacker News has contacted pCloud for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back. This is the third security incident targeting password management software this month alone. At the start of November 2026, mSeven Software urged customers to change their passwords, reset 2FA, and remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity associated with its mSecure password management application. Although the company did not provide any details as to what systems were compromised, whether customer data was accessed, and how many users were impacted, customers have since shared responses reportedly sent by mSeven that indicate an unknown threat actor "acquired an encrypted copy of a database containing information belonging to current and former users of the mSecure password management application." The email, however, stated that there is "no evidence that the unauthorized actor has accessed the confidential information stored within the database in the mSecure Cloud. Please note, this issue only pertains to users that were synching with the mSecure Cloud." Customers have also expressed dissatisfaction over the company's lack of transparency and explanations about how the breach took place. "Well it stinks that mSecure is completely silent here! Super unhelpful. I'm going on every website that has app reviews and giving mSecure the lowest rating. They're awful at handling this breach!," one user said. "I feel like even if our data is still secure, I still do not like that [sic] lack of transparency and communication the company has provided," another user said. "Not a good way to run any business, especially one where trust is involved with passwords and documents." On Wednesday, 1Password disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems after a threat actor compromised an employee's GitHub account and deployed malicious code to the company's backend services to steal some customer information. Although the access did not extend to customer password vaults or other secrets, 1Password has not revealed how the employee's account was compromised. It also provided no details on when the intruder gained access, was detected, and was subsequently locked out.
